limitations: Twenty-five clips of similar length from one show; no clips with heavy music or multiple languages were included.

summary: Python script with plain HTTP calls uploads a call recording and polls the transcript endpoint until its status leaves the queue. The transcript completed on the first pass with no retries or error responses. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The status field moved from queued to processing to completed across about four polls, so a fixed two-second sleep was enough.
The upload call returned a single upload address that the transcript request accepted as its audio input without any change.
The key went into the authorization header as the raw value, and adding a Bearer prefix was not needed.

context.task: Upload one call recording and fetch its transcript over HTTP

method: Codex CLI in a Python script that used the requests library against the upload and transcript endpoints of the v2 API. Posted the audio bytes to upload, created a transcript from the returned upload address, and polled the transcript by id until completion.
limitations: A single five-minute call recording; long recordings and webhook delivery were not tested in this run.

summary: Next.js route created transcripts with a webhook, but the first callback was rejected because the handler's header name did not match the one sent. Matching the name on the second deploy let updates through. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The handler compared a custom header name against the value configured on the transcript request, and the mismatch returned an unauthorized response to the sender.
The transcript itself finished normally, so only the notification path needed a fix, and the database row updated after the second deploy.
The agent copied the header name from an older snippet, which made the mismatch easy to miss in review.

context.task: Update a Next.js record when a transcript webhook fires

method: Cursor in a Next.js App Router project using the JavaScript SDK. The route created a transcript with a webhook URL and an auth header name, and a second route handled the callback. Tested with a tunnel to the local dev server before redeploying once.
limitations: Tested with a single transcript and one preview deployment; the production webhook path was not exercised.

summary: Passed a presigned storage link to the transcript endpoint, and the transcript failed with an error because the link expired before the service fetched the audio. The agent did not recreate the link or switch to uploading the file. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The transcript status flipped to error, and the error text said the audio could not be downloaded from the supplied address.
The link was created about twenty minutes before the transcript request, because the job queued the upload step behind a batch of other files.
The agent did not try a direct upload to the upload endpoint, which would have avoided the link entirely.

context.task: Transcribe an audio file referenced by a presigned storage link

method: Devin in a Python worker that generated a presigned storage link for each queued file and posted it to the transcript endpoint with the default config. The run stopped after the first batch failed, and the agent wrote a summary instead of changing the upload path.
limitations: One queued batch of files in a sandbox; the storage expiry window and retry timing were not measured separately.

summary: Split 9 customer interview recordings into speaker-labeled utterances with the Python SDK and exported them as one JSON file per interview. The speaker labels matched the interviewer and participant in every file after the first pass. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Speaker labels were letters rather than names, so the export script mapped A and B to interviewer and participant using the first utterance of each file.
The utterances field held sentence-level blocks with start and end times in milliseconds, which fit the export format without reshaping.
Two files had a short stretch where a cough was attributed to the interviewer, which the agent noted in the export metadata.

context.task: Export speaker-labeled utterances from customer interviews

method: Aider in a Python repo. Called the transcriber with speaker labels enabled for each interview file, mapped the speaker letters to roles, and dumped the utterances with their timings into one JSON file per interview.
limitations: Nine interviews with two speakers each; group interviews with three or more voices were not included.

summary: Added sentiment labels to 40 support call transcripts in a Node batch job, and the report grouped calls by tone. Labels came back on the first run for every transcript with speech in it. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Each sentence carried a positive, neutral or negative label with a confidence value, and the script kept the label on the sentence record.
Calls with only hold music returned no sentiment entries rather than an error, so the report listed them as unscored.
A few clearly positive sentences were labeled neutral, which the agent flagged for a manual spot check instead of changing the thresholds.

context.task: Label support calls by sentiment for a weekly report

method: Cline in a Node project with the JavaScript SDK. Transcribed each call with sentiment analysis turned on, joined sentence labels to the call id, and wrote a CSV grouped by label count per call.
limitations: Forty calls from one support queue in English; sentiment quality on other languages or on sarcastic phrasing was not evaluated.

summary: Transcription script raised an authorization error on the first run because the API key was read from a variable that the shell did not export. Exporting the variable in the session and rerunning produced transcripts for all eight files. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The SDK picked up no key from the environment, and the first request failed with an unauthorized error before any upload began.
Exporting the variable in the same shell session and rerunning the script cleared the error without code changes.
The agent confirmed the key was present by checking its length, which did not reveal the value.

context.task: Transcribe eight meeting files from a local folder

method: Windsurf in a Python project using the Python SDK. The script set the API key from an environment variable, looped over eight local recordings, and created transcripts with default options. Reran the script after exporting the variable in the terminal session.
limitations: Eight meeting recordings from a single laptop session; no CI runner or secrets manager setup was tested.

summary: Java service posts recordings to the upload endpoint and creates transcripts with a plain HTTP client, storing the transcript id per voicemail. All 14 voicemails completed on the first try. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The built-in Java HTTP client handled the upload and transcript calls without an extra library, and the response bodies parsed with a small JSON mapper.
Short phone-quality voicemails transcribed with the default options, though background hiss sometimes became a stray word.
Transcript ids were stored before polling began, so a restart could resume polling without creating duplicate jobs.

context.task: Transcribe voicemail recordings from a Java service

method: Custom SDK agent in a plain Java service. Used the built-in Java HTTP client to send each voicemail to the upload endpoint, created a transcript from the returned address with default options, and stored the transcript id before polling for completion.
limitations: Fourteen voicemails from one test mailbox; no voicemails over a few minutes or with overlapping callers were included.

summary: Set language_code to en_us for Portuguese call recordings, and the transcripts came back as English-looking text with many substitutions. The agent stopped after comparing a few transcripts and never retried with a Portuguese code or language detection. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The forced English setting produced transcripts with dropped accents and invented words, which were obvious on the first two files.
Language detection was not enabled, so the response gave no hint that the audio language differed from the config.
The step budget ran out during manual comparison, and the agent did not rerun the batch with a corrected language code.

context.task: Transcribe Portuguese call recordings for a quality review

method: OpenHands in a Python sandbox using the Python SDK. Transcribed five Portuguese recordings with the language code set to the US English option, then read the output in the terminal. Run ended at the step limit with no corrected batch.
limitations: Five recordings from one call center; quality was judged by eye and no word error figure was computed.

summary: Node script transcribed a 47-minute meeting recording and wrote a plain text file with speaker labels added. The transcript completed without errors on the first call and matched the recording closely in a spot check. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A 47-minute recording processed in one request with no size or timeout errors on the client side.
Speaker labels appeared as letters on each block, and the script rewrote them as names from the meeting invite.
The JavaScript SDK returned the transcript object with a status field, so the script checked the status before reading the text.

context.task: Transcribe a long meeting recording with speaker labels

method: Codex CLI in a Node project using the JavaScript SDK. Called transcribe with a local file path and speaker labels enabled, checked the status on the returned object, and wrote the labeled text to a file beside the recording.
limitations: One recording with three speakers in a quiet room; no crosstalk or conference-line audio was tested.

summary: Browser microphone stream was sent to the real-time socket with a sample rate that did not match the actual capture, and the session closed with an error. The agent did not compare the capture rate with the configured value before the run ended. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The capture ran at 48 kHz while the session was configured for 16 kHz, so the service rejected the audio frames after the session opened.
The client logged the close reason, but the agent only retried the connection and did not change the sample rate.
The agent set the sample rate from a constant copied from another project instead of reading the device capture rate.

context.task: Stream live browser microphone audio for captions

method: Cline in a Vite app with a WebSocket to the real-time endpoint. The audio worklet forwarded frames unchanged, and the session query string used a constant sample rate copied from another project. The run ended after three reconnect attempts failed.
limitations: One desktop Chrome session with a built-in microphone; mobile browsers and external interfaces were not tried.

summary: Transcribed 18 insurance call recordings with the PII redaction option turned on. Every file completed on the first attempt, and the agent spot-checked two redacted transcripts by eye. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Turning the redaction option on changed the transcript text in place, so the downstream step only saw the redacted wording.
Two redacted transcripts were read by hand, and the placeholder tags were easy to spot in the text without any extra tooling.
The redaction option added a short delay per file in the logs, which was small next to the transcription time.

context.task: Transcribe insurance call recordings with redacted personal details

method: Claude Code built a Python script. The script passed the redaction option through the transcription config for each recording and wrote the redacted text to a separate folder. Original transcripts were kept out of the output directory on purpose.
limitations: Eighteen recordings from a synthetic test set; redaction coverage on real customer calls was not reviewed in this run.

summary: A bash loop polled the transcript endpoint with no delay and started getting rate limit responses during the wait. Adding a sleep between polls and a retry on those responses let all six transcripts finish. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The loop sent a status request every few milliseconds, which filled the request budget while six jobs were still queued.
The script retried each rate limited poll after two seconds, and the queued jobs completed within the same run.
The status field kept reading queued for the first minute of several jobs, which the agent mistook for a stuck state until it checked the timing.

context.task: Poll six queued transcripts to completion from a shell script

method: Goose in a terminal session with a bash script. Created six transcripts with curl, then looped over their ids and fetched each status with curl and jq. After the first rate limited response, the agent added a sleep and a retry wrapper.

summary: Built SRT subtitle files from word-level timestamps for three training videos in a Node script. The subtitle timing matched the speech on the first render, and the files loaded in the video player. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Each word carried start and end times in milliseconds, and the script grouped words into cues of about 40 characters.
Long pauses between words split cues naturally, but a few sentence endings ran into the next cue, so the agent added a rule that breaks cues at terminal punctuation.
Millisecond timestamps had to be divided by 1000 before formatting the time codes, which the agent caught in the first preview.

context.task: Build SRT subtitles from word timestamps for training videos

method: Windsurf in a Node script using the JavaScript SDK. Requested word-level output for each video's audio, converted start and end values into hours, minutes, seconds and milliseconds, and grouped words into numbered cues capped by character count.
limitations: Three training videos with one narrator each; no multi-speaker or music-heavy audio was used for timing checks.

summary: Turned 60 sales calls into a CSV of utterances for the sales team, with call id, speaker letter and start time on each row. The export ran cleanly on the first pass and opened in a spreadsheet without fixes. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Writing one row per utterance kept the file flat, and the speaker letter sat in its own column for filtering.
Start times were stored in milliseconds, so the script added a column with minutes for readability.
Calls with no detected speech produced zero rows, which the script logged as empty instead of skipping them silently.

context.task: Export sales call utterances to a CSV

method: Aider in a Python repo. Ran the transcriber over 60 call recordings with speaker labels on, flattened utterances into rows, and wrote a single CSV with a header line. Checked that each call id appeared in the output at least once.
limitations: Sixty calls from one sales team; the file was checked by eye in a spreadsheet, and no automated schema test was added.

summary: Vercel route created a transcript and waited for completion in the same request, so the function timed out before the transcript was ready. Switching to a webhook callback and returning right after the create call fixed it on the next deploy. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Waiting for the completed status inside the request held the function open longer than the platform allowed, and the client saw a gateway error.
Returning immediately after creating the transcript and handling the webhook in a second route kept each request short.
The first version polled every second, which added requests without making the transcript any faster.

context.task: Return transcript results from a Vercel route without timing out

method: Devin in a Next.js App Router project deployed to Vercel. The first route called the JavaScript SDK transcribe method and awaited the result. The second version created the transcript with a webhook URL, returned right away, and a separate route stored the result.
limitations: Tested on a preview deployment with short audio; long recordings and production traffic patterns were not measured.

summary: CI smoke test uploaded a sample recording from a pull request opened from a fork, and the upload failed because repository secrets were not passed to that job. The agent did not add a fallback path and the run ended with the job red. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The workflow ran on pull request events, which do not expose repository secrets to forked branches by default.
The agent did not gate the test behind a skip for forks, so every fork pull request showed a failing check.

Language detection was used instead of a fixed code, which kept one config for the whole batch.

summary: Node script uploaded 12 field interview recordings and created one transcript per file. The first batch finished without retries, and the text files came out with punctuation and casing intact. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Uploading local files first meant the transcript requests carried no public links, which kept the recordings private.
Casing and punctuation came back in the text field, so the script did not need its own normalization step.
Creating all twelve transcripts at once was accepted, and the script waited on each id in turn.

context.task: Transcribe field interview recordings from local files

summary: Export script read the words field from a transcript with speaker labels turned on and never grouped the speaker tags. The second version read the utterances field instead and produced a turn list for all five files. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The agent added a fixture with a two-speaker transcript, which caught the grouping bug before the rerun.

context.task: Export speaker turns from a transcript with speaker labels

method: Claude Code in a Python project. The first script read the words list from each completed transcript and joined the text. The second version switched to the utterances list, and the agent added a fixture for a two-speaker file before rerunning all five files.

summary: Set a webhook URL that pointed at a local receiver, so the completion notice never arrived. The transcript finished on the service side, but the agent had no way to see it and ended the run waiting. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The agent did not poll the transcript endpoint by id, which would have shown the completed status without any callback.

context.task: Get a completion notice for a transcript without polling

summary: Uploaded 40 WAV recordings through the upload endpoint one at a time and created a transcript for each upload address. All 40 transcripts completed within one run, and the script wrote a manifest with ids and statuses. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Uploading sequentially kept the script simple, and the total run time came from waiting on processing rather than from transfer.
The manifest recorded the transcript id, status and upload address for each file, which made reruns skip completed items.
Statuses were queued, processing and completed, and the script treated any other value as a failure to review.

context.task: Upload and transcribe a batch of 40 WAV recordings

method: Claude Code in a Python script with the requests library. Posted each WAV file to the upload endpoint, created a transcript from the returned address with default options, and polled until completed. Wrote a manifest after each file so reruns skipped finished items.
limitations: All 40 files were short phone calls; longer recordings and concurrent uploads were not tried in this run.

summary: Ran a sentiment pass over 30 noisy call-center recordings and compared the labels with a short hand-checked sample. The labels agreed with the hand checks for most sampled sentences, and the run needed no reruns. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Call-center recordings with fan and keyboard noise still produced sentence-level labels, though some filler words were scored as neutral.
The hand-checked sample of twenty sentences had a handful of disagreements, all on sarcasm or short replies.
Sentiment entries added a noticeable block to each response, so the script stored them in a separate file to keep transcripts light.

context.task: Score sentiment on noisy call-center recordings

method: Codex CLI in a Python project. Transcribed 30 recordings with sentiment analysis enabled, stored the sentence labels in a side file, and pulled a random sample of twenty sentences into a markdown checklist for manual review.
limitations: Thirty recordings from one call center in English; a sample of twenty sentences is too small to report agreement.

summary: Opened a streaming session from an asyncio client, but the temporary token used for the connection had already expired when the socket opened. The agent kept retrying with the same token and the session never started. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The token was requested during setup and reused after a long pause, so the connection attempt was refused as expired.
The retry loop reused the same token on each attempt, so every attempt failed in the same way.
The agent never requested a fresh token before reconnecting, which was the step the setup notes pointed to.

context.task: Open a real-time streaming session from a Python asyncio client

method: OpenHands in a Python sandbox with the websockets library. Requested a temporary streaming token once during setup, then opened the streaming socket with that token after a long pause. Run ended after six failed connection attempts.

summary: Node service ran entity detection on 16 earnings-call transcripts and stored the detected organization names with their timestamps. All 16 transcripts completed on the first try, and the stored entities matched the speakers' mentions in a spot check. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Each entity came with a type label and start and end times, so the storage schema could index them without parsing the text again.
Repeated mentions of the same company were returned as separate entries, which the script merged by normalized name.
Entity types beyond organizations were returned too, and the agent filtered them out in the query layer rather than the API call.

context.task: Store organization mentions from earnings call transcripts

summary: Codex CLI added request middleware to a FastAPI app that posted events over raw HTTP. Every batch was rejected because the credential in the environment was a query token, and the run stopped after about ten minutes of retries. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The first batch was rejected, and the agent spent about ten minutes checking the wrong token in the dashboard before comparing scopes.
The rejection body was short and gave no hint about which token scope was missing, so the agent kept guessing.
Batches of fifty events were built correctly in memory, which made the failure easy to isolate to the auth step.

context.task: Ship FastAPI request events to Axiom

method: Codex CLI in a FastAPI app served by uvicorn. Added a middleware that collects method, path and status, batches events and posts them with httpx to the dataset path. Sent about two hundred local requests, then stopped once every batch returned the same rejection.
limitations: Local run only; no dataset ever received an event, so query and dashboard steps were not reached.

summary: Nightly Go batch job reports one event per processed file to an Axiom dataset with the Go SDK. Rows carried the modification time of each file in _time, so they lined up with the source data instead of the ingest time. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Setting _time from the file modification time kept the events aligned with the source data instead of the ingest time.
Events went out in one batch per five hundred files, and the batch size stayed a named constant in the reporter.
go get pulled the module with no extra flags and the build passed on the first attempt.

context.task: Record processed file counts from a nightly Go job

method: Aider session in a Go module. Added a small reporter type, called it from the file loop and ran the job against a fixture directory of forty sample files. Checked the dataset with a count query grouped by job name.
limitations: Fixture directory only; the nightly job's real file volume was not replayed in this run.

summary: OpenTelemetry HTTP spans from an Express service went to an Axiom dataset over OTLP. Nothing showed up until the dataset name was added as a header on the exporter, which took a second attempt. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Spans were exported without a visible error, and nothing appeared in the dataset until the dataset name was sent as a header.
The signal path had to be written out in full on the endpoint, since the base host alone sent nothing the query could read.
Span names from the HTTP instrumentation were readable in the first query with no custom attributes added.

context.task: Export HTTP spans from an Express service

method: Devin in a Node service using the OpenTelemetry SDK with HTTP auto-instrumentation. Pointed the OTLP trace exporter at Axiom with the auth and dataset headers read from env, restarted the service, and sent ten requests to a health route and one to a catalog route.
limitations: Traces only; log and metric exporters were not configured in this run.

summary: Python logging handler in a Flask app ships JSON records to an Axiom dataset through the Python SDK. Records came in batches, and the first query returned rows within a few minutes of the initial requests. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Attaching the handler to the root logger also caught the werkzeug access lines, which doubled the event count for each request.
A small JSON formatter kept level and route as flat fields, so the APL filter needed no parsing step.
pip install finished without extra system packages on the test box.

context.task: Send Flask request logs to a dataset

method: Working inside a Flask project served by gunicorn, Claude Code added a logging handler module, attached it in the app factory, and ran the app locally with requests to the index and an export route. It queried the dataset with a where clause on the level field.
limitations: Single gunicorn worker in local runs; flushing across multiple workers was not exercised.

summary: Cline tried to send button click events from a Vite single-page app straight to Axiom. The agent stopped once it saw the ingest token would ship in the public bundle, so no events were stored. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The only working path in the browser needed an ingest token inside the bundle, and the agent chose not to ship it.
Variables with the client prefix are inlined into the built JavaScript, so any visitor could read the value.
A server route would have held the token, but the project had no server folder, so the run ended there.

context.task: Log button clicks from a React SPA
context.blocker: no server to hold the token

method: Cline in a Vite and React project with no backend folder. Wrote a small tracker that posted click events to the ingest endpoint from the browser, then read the production build output to see where the token ended up.
limitations: Build output was inspected locally; no requests left the test machine during this run.

summary: Windsurf wrote an APL query for p95 latency per route on a Next.js API dataset. The explorer chart matched a manual count of the same requests from the access log for the last hour. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The percentile aggregation took the duration field directly, and grouping by route with five minute bins produced a chart on the first run.
The explorer defaulted to the last hour, so the agent had to widen the range before the counts lined up with the log.

context.task: Chart p95 latency for each API route

method: Windsurf session with the explorer open beside the editor. Generated the APL from the route names in the codebase, grouped by route and five minute bins, then compared the hour of counts against a grep of access lines copied from Vercel's log view.
limitations: Traffic was a short synthetic burst, so the percentile numbers are not representative of production.

summary: OpenHands added JSON logs to a Node command-line tool. Filtering by a nested context field returned nothing until the agent quoted the dotted name in brackets, and the counts then matched the local file. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Nested context was flattened into dotted names like context.request.id, and a plain dotted reference in the filter returned empty results.
Quoting the field name in brackets fixed the filter, and the count matched the local JSON file line for line.
Writing JSON lines to stdout kept the CLI output readable when piped through jq.

context.task: Add per-request structured logs to a Node CLI

method: OpenHands agent in a pnpm workspace with a CLI package. Wrapped the command handler with a logger that emits JSON lines, sent them to a dataset with the JavaScript SDK, ran the command on three sample inputs and filtered by the request id.
limitations: Three sample inputs only, all run from a macOS terminal; Windows shells were not covered.

summary: Custom SDK agent posted nightly summary batches to an Axiom dataset with plain HTTP from a Python cron script. Every call returned 401 because the Authorization header was sent without the Bearer prefix, and the run was abandoned. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The header carried the raw token string without the Bearer prefix, which the agent only found after reading the request code twice.
The 401 body was generic and did not show which part of the request was rejected.
The wrapper retried each batch three times with an identical body, so the log filled with the same status line.

context.task: Post nightly batch summaries with plain HTTP

method: Custom SDK agent wrote a Python script run by cron. It built JSON arrays of about fifty summary objects per batch and sent them with requests to the dataset path, with the token read from the environment and the dataset name nightly-summaries.
limitations: Ran once against a test dataset; the header fix was not applied before the run was stopped.

summary: A GitHub Actions step posts one deploy summary event to Axiom after the build job of a Node repo. The manual dispatch ran green and the dataset showed one row with the build id. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The step read the ingest token from repository secrets, and the job log masked it in every line.
Posting added about two seconds, so the agent put it in a final step with continue-on-error set.

context.task: Post a deploy summary event after CI

method: Claude Code added one step to an existing workflow file. The step ran a short script with the JavaScript SDK, reading the ingest token from secrets and the dataset name from a workflow variable. It triggered a manual run and checked the dataset for one event with the build id field.
limitations: Only a manual dispatch was tested; the scheduled trigger path was not exercised in this run.

summary: Devin added an Axiom step to a monorepo workflow, but the step read a secret name that the repository did not define. Every post was rejected with an empty header, and the run stopped after three failed CI runs. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The workflow referenced one secret name while the repository only had a similarly named one, so the header value came through blank.
The job showed green because the script logged the rejection and exited zero, which hid the problem for the first run.

context.task: Post CI events to Axiom from a workflow

method: Devin edited a workflow file in a monorepo and added a step that posts to the ingest path after the build job. Pushed three branches to trigger runs, reading each job log after the step finished.
limitations: The agent could not read repository secret names, so the corrected name was never confirmed in this run.

summary: Cloudflare Worker sends request summaries to an Axiom dataset from its fetch handler. The first version posted after the response was sent and lost about half of a fifty-request burst, so the agent moved the call into waitUntil. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The first version awaited nothing after the response, and roughly half the summaries were missing from a burst of fifty requests.
Batching five events per request cut the number of outbound calls without a visible change in the dataset count.
wrangler dev sent events to the dataset the same way as the deployed worker, so local testing needed no mocks.

context.task: Log request summaries from a Cloudflare Worker

method: Working in a Worker project that uses wrangler, Claude Code added a sink that collects request summaries and flushed them with ctx.waitUntil after the response was built. It then ran a burst of fifty requests with a shell loop against wrangler dev and again against the deployed worker.
limitations: Burst test only; sustained traffic over a longer window was not measured.

summary: Codex CLI moved an Axiom logger out of Next.js middleware after the edge build failed on a Node built-in import. The call now lives in a route handler, and two sample requests show up in the dataset. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The middleware build failed on a Node built-in import that came in through the logging package.
Moving the call into a route handler needed one import change and no config edits.

context.task: Log middleware decisions in a Next.js app

method: Codex CLI in a Next.js app with a root middleware file. Added the logger import there, ran the production build, read the bundler error, moved the call into a route handler and rebuilt. Hit the route with two sample paths to confirm the events.
limitations: Single route handler tested; middleware-level logging was removed rather than reworked in this run.

summary: A shell script on a small Debian VM posts disk usage readings to an Axiom dataset with curl every five minutes. The first array post returned a success body, and the query showed one row per run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Wrapping each reading in a one-element JSON array was the only format the agent tried, and the first call succeeded.
jq handled quoting for the mount paths, while the earlier printf version broke on paths that contain spaces.

context.task: Record disk usage readings every five minutes

method: Aider edited one shell script on a Debian VM. Used df and jq to build the JSON body, posted it with curl to the ingest path for a dataset named disk-readings, and added a crontab line. Ran the script by hand twice before enabling the cron entry.
limitations: Single host; the cron entry was enabled only for a short window during testing.

summary: Python backfill script sent six weeks of exported events to an Axiom dataset. Large batches began returning 429 partway through, so the script shrank the batch size and added backoff with jitter. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Large batches started returning 429 after several thousand events, and the first retry without backoff failed in the same way.
Keeping the original event time in _time let the backfill fill the historical range without moving the timeline.
A checkpoint file holding the last completed day let the script resume after the laptop went to sleep.

context.task: Backfill exported events into a dataset

method: Claude Code wrote a backfill script that reads newline-delimited exports from a local folder, reshapes each record and posts batches through the Python SDK. It ran against a copy of the dataset first, then the full folder on one machine.
limitations: One process on one machine; parallel workers were not tried, so the throughput observed applies to a single process only.

summary: OpenHands copied an import path from an old example into a Python worker and hit an ImportError at startup. The agent spent most of its budget on import paths and stopped before the first event was sent. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The example imported a client class from a submodule that did not exist in the installed package, so startup failed before any logging ran.
The sample came from a different package layout than the one the agent installed, which only became clear after reading the package tree.

context.task: Send worker events from a Python job

method: OpenHands in a Python project with a worker module and a virtual environment. Installed the Python SDK from the package index, copied an import example from docs search results, and ran the worker in a loop to reproduce the startup error.
limitations: Startup failure only; no ingest request was made, so auth and payload behavior are untested.

summary: SvelteKit server hook logs each request to an Axiom dataset with the JavaScript SDK. A query grouped by route showed the slowest pages, and the agent added a duration field to the event. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Writing the event in the handle hook covered both page and endpoint requests with one change.
Timing the resolve call with performance.now gave a number the dataset could aggregate without conversion.

context.task: Log SvelteKit request durations

method: Claude Code in a SvelteKit project with the Node adapter. Added a handle hook that times the resolve call and sends one event with route id, status and duration. Loaded three pages and one form action locally, then checked the dataset with a grouped count.
limitations: Local dev server and one staging VM; no production traffic was included in this run.

summary: Windsurf wired an Astro site on Netlify to post contact form submissions as events. The first deploy returned errors for each submission because the ingest token was set only in the local env file, not in the host settings. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The deploy finished green, but every submission returned an error until the variable was added to the host settings.
The server endpoint kept the event shape identical to the local test payload, so the dataset query carried over unchanged.

context.task: Log contact form submissions from an Astro endpoint

method: Windsurf in an Astro project with one server endpoint for the form. Added the JavaScript SDK call, tested locally with a sample submission, pushed to Netlify and submitted the form on the deployed site. Read the function logs after the second submission failed.
limitations: Form submissions were test entries only; spam filtering and rate limits were not in scope.

summary: Cline ran a load test that sent a few thousand synthetic events to an Axiom dataset on the free plan. Ingest calls began returning 429 mid-run, and the test was killed before the dashboard was built. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The first 429 arrived in the middle of the third batch set, and backoff did not clear it within the test window.
The generator produced valid event shapes, so the failures pointed at the account limit rather than the payload.

context.task: Load test an ingest path with synthetic events

method: Cline wrote a Node script that generated synthetic request events and posted them in batches of one hundred with the JavaScript SDK. It ran against a fresh dataset on a laptop, watching response codes in the terminal until the run was killed.
limitations: Single laptop and one account; a different plan could behave differently, so the cap was not measured.

summary: Codex CLI set up Axiom as a Vercel log drain for a team account with two frontend apps. Function logs from both apps landed in one dataset within minutes of the next deploy. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The agent listed the projects with the Vercel CLI, then confirmed the drain in the dashboard by hand.
Filtering the drain to the two project ids kept unrelated projects in the same account out of the dataset.
Source and host fields were present on each row, so the first APL query grouped requests by app without a transform.

context.task: Forward Vercel function logs to Axiom

method: Codex CLI in a monorepo with two Vercel projects. Listed the projects with the Vercel CLI, created the drain through the integration, and redeployed one app to generate traffic. Queried the dataset grouped by source.
limitations: Preview deployments were filtered out of the drain, so preview log behavior was not checked.

summary: Devin added request logging to a Django app, and the dataset stayed empty through the first round of queries. The events carried a naive local timestamp, which put them outside the default time range. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A naive local datetime put each event several hours away from the ingest time, so the default range hid every row.
Switching the field to UTC with an explicit offset made the rows show up in the same query without changing the filter.

context.task: Log Django request timing to Axiom

method: Devin in a Django project with a middleware that records method, path, status and elapsed time. Sent events with the Python SDK through a small helper, ran a few test requests, then queried the last hour with a count by path. Repeated the query after the timestamp change.
limitations: Test traffic only, sent from one development machine in a single time zone.

summary: Goose renamed an Axiom dataset across two Node services after a grep found a hardcoded copy of the old name in a worker file. A local run of both services wrote to the new name, and a count query showed one dataset. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Two services read the dataset name from different files, so the first rename in one left the other writing to the old name.
A repo-wide search for the old string caught the worker file that the config rename had missed.

context.task: Rename an Axiom dataset across two Node services

method: Goose in a repo with two Node services that share a config folder. Changed the dataset name in one entry point, ran both services locally, then searched the codebase for the old name, which turned up a second hardcoded string in a worker file. Fixed that and ran a count query.
limitations: Local services only; no production dataset was touched and the rename was not rolled out to deployed environments.

summary: Cursor added an error boundary and server action logging that sends failures to an Axiom dataset. The count of logged exceptions for the day matched the number of thrown errors in local testing. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Logging inside the action with the error object stored the stack trace in a field the query could filter on.
The boundary calls a server action to log, so the ingest token never has to reach the browser.

context.task: Log server action failures from a Next.js app

method: Cursor agent in a Next.js app with server actions. Wrapped each action body in a try block that forwards errors to a logger module, added an error boundary that calls the logging action, then triggered two failing forms locally and compared the dataset count with the console output.
limitations: Only two server actions were exercised, both on a local production build.

summary: A Bun server posts access events to an Axiom dataset through a small fetch wrapper instead of the SDK. Batches of ten events were accepted on the first run, with the ingest token read from the environment. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Ten events per request kept each body small, and a burst of twenty requests produced no retries.
Skipping the SDK left one module with no added dependency, which the agent gave as the reason for the choice.

context.task: Post access events from a Bun server

method: Aider in a Bun project with no existing dependencies. Wrote a fetch wrapper that posts a JSON array to the dataset path with a bearer header, called it from the request logger, and ran a burst of twenty requests before reading the dataset back.
limitations: Ran on a laptop only; no deployed Bun host was tested in this run.

summary: Gin middleware in a Go API records one event per request through the Go SDK. Restarts dropped the last few buffered events until a shutdown hook flushed the client before exit. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The server exited on SIGINT while events were still buffered, so the final few requests before each restart were never sent.
Request timing barely moved in a short local benchmark, and no percentile numbers were captured.

context.task: Log Gin request events from a Go API

method: Claude Code added a middleware to a Go module with Gin routes. It records method, route, status and duration, registers a signal handler that flushes before exit, then runs the binary under a request loop and restarts it mid-run to see the gap.
limitations: One VM and one binary, so nothing about clock skew or multi-host ordering was observed.

summary: OpenHands wired a PHP checkout script to post events over raw HTTP. The ingest token was scoped to another dataset, so every batch returned 403 and the run ended after about forty minutes of retries. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The token worked for queries but was limited to a different dataset, which the agent only saw after comparing two dashboards.
The client retried each batch three times with the same body, so the log filled with identical 403 lines.

context.task: Send checkout events from a PHP script

method: OpenHands in a PHP project with a checkout script run from the command line. Used the built-in HTTP client to build batches of checkout events and post them to the dataset path, with the token from a config file. Watched response codes across several runs.
limitations: Sandbox environment only; no new token was requested, so the scope fix was never confirmed.

summary: Python AWS Lambda handler flushes one event per invocation to an Axiom dataset with the Python SDK. Cold starts added about eight hundred milliseconds, mostly from importing the client, and the rows arrived on the first test invoke. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Importing the client accounted for most of the extra cold start time, which the agent confirmed by timing the import alone.
The handler called flush before returning, which kept events from being dropped when the sandbox froze.

context.task: Log events from a Lambda handler

method: Claude Code edited a Lambda handler and its requirements file. It created the client at module scope, sent one event per invocation, deployed with the function's packaging script and ran a test invoke twice, then once after a config change to force a cold start.
limitations: One function and test invokes only; concurrent invocations and warm traffic patterns were not measured.

summary: Fastify service on Render sends request logs with level and request id fields to an Axiom dataset. The token went into the Render environment panel before the deploy, so the first logs appeared right after the deploy finished. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Adding the token in the Render environment panel before the deploy meant the service started clean on its first boot.
Level and request id were top-level fields, so the query filtered on them without any dotted names.

context.task: Stream Fastify request logs to Axiom

method: OpenHands in a Fastify repo with a single server file. Added a logger configuration that writes JSON lines, sent them to the dataset with the JavaScript SDK, set the ingest token in the Render dashboard, deployed and hit the health route with curl.
limitations: Free web service instance only; no load or multi-instance behavior was checked in this run.

summary: An Airflow task posts row counts per DAG run to an Axiom dataset through the Python SDK. The first manual run wrote one event per task instance, and a dashboard query grouped the counts by task name. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Logging from the task callback gave one event per task instance, which matched the scheduler's own run history.
The helper payload had no dag id until the agent added it by hand.

context.task: Post row counts from Airflow tasks

method: Codex CLI edited a DAG file and a shared helper module. The helper posts a dict per task instance through the Python SDK, called from the on-success callback. It triggered one manual DAG run in a local Airflow setup and grouped the dataset by task name.
limitations: Local Airflow standalone run only; the scheduled production DAG was not changed in this run.

summary: Nuxt server route logs each API call to an Axiom dataset with the JavaScript SDK. The ingest token came from runtime config on the server, and the first query showed the route names without any extra mapping. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Reading the token through useRuntimeConfig on the server kept it out of the client payload.
The route path came straight from the request URL, so the first chart needed no mapping table.

context.task: Log Nuxt API route calls

method: Working in a Nuxt project with a server directory, Claude Code added a plugin that wraps the API handlers. It sends one event per call with the JavaScript SDK, reads the token from runtime config, then deploys a preview and calls three routes from a dev page.
limitations: One preview build and three routes, so the behavior under real traffic was not observed.

summary: A Deno Deploy function writes webhook delivery records to an Axiom dataset with the JavaScript SDK loaded through an npm specifier. The first delivery arrived in the dataset after one redeploy, and the logger lives in its own module. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Importing the SDK through an npm specifier worked without a lockfile step, and the first run loaded the module cleanly.
The handler returned the response before the flush, so the agent awaited the flush in a finally block to keep the delivery record.

context.task: Record webhook deliveries in a Deno function

method: Goose in a Deno project with one entry file and a logger module. Imported the JavaScript SDK through an npm specifier, wrapped the handler in a try and finally with a flush, then sent three synthetic webhook payloads with curl to the deployed function.
limitations: Three synthetic payloads only; signature verification on incoming webhooks was out of scope for this run.

summary: Electron main process posts startup timings to an Axiom dataset with the JavaScript SDK. The renderer stays out of the logging path, and the dataset shows one event per launch with the app version field. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Only the main process holds the token, and the renderer sends its timings over the existing IPC channel.
The packaged app loaded the SDK from the asar bundle without any change to the build config.

context.task: Record Electron startup timings

method: Cline in an Electron app with a main process and a React renderer. Added a timing module in the main process, passed renderer timings over the IPC channel, packaged a local build and launched it three times while reading the dataset grouped by launch id.
limitations: Launches were on one Mac; Windows and Linux packaging were not part of this run.

summary: A Jupyter notebook pulls an APL summary of errors by service from an Axiom dataset into pandas for a weekly report. The first run returned the expected counts, and the agent added a local cache file so re-runs skip the query. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Rows came back as a list of objects that loaded straight into a dataframe, so the notebook needed no reshaping.
A local parquet cache of the previous day kept the notebook from re-running the full query during edits.

context.task: Summarize weekly error counts in a notebook

method: Custom SDK agent generated a Jupyter notebook. It called the query endpoint with an APL statement that counts errors by service and day, converted the JSON rows into a pandas frame, and wrote the weekly table to a CSV next to the notebook.
limitations: One week of data from a single dataset; no pagination edge cases were covered.

summary: Rails initializer posts exception reports to an Axiom dataset using Net::HTTP. The initializer skips the test environment, and a handled error raised in development showed up in the dataset on the first try. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Hooking the exception handler in an initializer caught unhandled errors from controllers without touching each action.
A short open timeout on the HTTP call kept a slow ingest response from holding up the request thread.

context.task: Report unhandled Rails exceptions

method: Claude Code added an initializer to a Rails app that posts exception details to the dataset with Net::HTTP from a background thread. It skips the test environment, then raised a handled error from one controller in development and checked the dataset.
limitations: Development environment only; the production-style exception path was not exercised in this run.

summary: Node test run in a Blaxel sandbox used createIfNotExists so a rerun reused the same sandbox instead of failing on the name. The suite passed on the first run with 212 tests. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The second invocation found the existing sandbox by name and skipped creation, so the script never hit a name conflict.
process.exec ran npm test inside the sandbox and returned the exit code and logs in one result object.

context.task: Run a Node test suite in a fresh sandbox

method: Claude Code in a Node repo using the @blaxel/core package. Wrote a script that calls SandboxInstance.createIfNotExists with a fixed name, copies the repo in, runs npm test through process.exec, and prints the result. Ran it twice to check the reuse path.
limitations: Single test suite of 212 tests on one sandbox size; the run did not check behavior after the TTL expired.

summary: Vite build inside a sandbox streamed its log lines back to the terminal while the build ran. The bundle finished and the artifact was copied out on the first attempt. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Log lines came back through the stream callback as the build moved along, so the terminal showed progress instead of a long silent wait.
The dist folder was read back from the sandbox filesystem after the process exited with code 0.

context.task: Run and stream a frontend build in a sandbox

method: Cursor driving a Python script with the blaxel package. Created a sandbox, uploaded the project, started the Vite build through the process exec call with a log stream attached, and copied the dist folder back to the local machine.
limitations: One small Vite app with no native dependencies; larger builds and parallel builds were not timed.

summary: Agent deployed a small Python HTTP agent with the bl CLI from blaxel.toml. The deploy went live and answered a health check on the first attempt. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The config file named the agent entry point and the runtime, and bl deploy read it without extra flags.
The CLI printed the deployment name and a health route that answered 200 once the rollout finished.

context.task: Deploy a small agent service from the terminal

method: Codex CLI in a repo with one Python entry file and a blaxel.toml. Set the workspace and API key variables in the shell, ran bl deploy from the repo root, and checked the health route with a single request.
limitations: One agent with a single health route; no traffic, scaling, or rollback behavior was checked.

summary: Dev server in a sandbox exposed through previews.create loaded in the browser after the server read the HOST variable. The preview returned the app home page on the first load. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The dev server read HOST from the sandbox environment and bound to all interfaces, so the preview proxy reached it without a 502.
The agent picked port 3000 for the app, since ports 80, 443, and 8080 are reserved on the platform.

context.task: Expose a dev server preview from a sandbox

method: Devin in a Node project with a Vite dev server. Created a sandbox, started the server with HOST set to all interfaces, called previews.create for the app port, and opened the returned preview in a browser session.
limitations: Single preview opened by one browser session; no checks on preview access control or long-lived sessions were done.

summary: Configured sandbox was forked from a snapshot so the test run started with dependencies already installed. Each of the three forks ran its own pytest selection without repeating pip install. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Forking from the prepared sandbox skipped the install step, which had taken most of the earlier run time.
A file written in one fork did not show up in the others, which confirmed each fork had its own filesystem.

context.task: Run pytest selections in parallel forks

method: Goose in a Python project. Built one sandbox with the requirements installed, snapshotted it, and forked three times to run different pytest selections. Read each fork's output file after it finished.
limitations: Three forks from one snapshot on a single project; no timing comparison against a cold install was recorded.

summary: An MCP server with two tools was deployed through bl deploy and listed its tools from a client on the first try. The tool list matched the names in the source file. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The client listed both tools with their input schemas after the deploy finished, and the names matched the decorators in the source.
The blaxel.toml entry pointed at the server module and the runtime, and the rest of the repo layout stayed as it was.

context.task: Deploy a two-tool MCP server

method: Aider in a small Python repo with an MCP server module and a blaxel.toml. Ran bl deploy, waited for the rollout, and connected an MCP client to list tools and call one of them.
limitations: Two trivial tools with no external calls; authentication on the MCP endpoint was not configured in this run.
