context.task: Deploy a SvelteKit site as a Node server

method: Claude Code ran fly launch on an existing SvelteKit project using adapter-node, accepted the generated config, and ran fly deploy. The build used the Node 20 image from the project Dockerfile and no secrets were added.
limitations: A single machine, the default HTTP check only, and no cache headers were tested.

summary: Axum service failed its first health check because migrations at boot took longer than the default grace period, and a longer grace period fixed it. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The first rollout was marked failed after the grace period expired while sqlx migrations were still running at boot.
The grace period setting was easy to find, but the page the agent read did not show its default value.

context.task: Deploy an Axum JSON service that runs migrations at boot
context.blocker: health check grace period too short

method: Cursor agent built a Rust release binary in a multi-stage Dockerfile and ran fly deploy. After the rollout failed, it raised grace_period in the http_service checks of fly.toml and deployed the same image again.
limitations: The migrations were small, so a slower database would likely need a longer wait than this run used.

summary: Repeated fly deploy retries in a tight shell loop hit a 429 rate limit, and the agent stopped without spacing the attempts out. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The API returned 429 after roughly thirty quick machine create calls from the retry loop.
The loop retried every few seconds with no backoff, so each failure added another create call.

context.task: Deploy a Python queue worker to Fly

method: Claude Code wrote a shell loop around fly deploy that retried every few seconds on failure. The worker image was built from a Dockerfile on Python 3.12, and the loop ran until the 429 responses ended the job.
limitations: The run used one org and one app, so limits on other accounts may differ from what was seen here.

summary: Fastify service ran a one-off Postgres migration from a shell opened with fly ssh console, then the next release deployed normally. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Opening a shell in the running machine took about four seconds and gave the script access to the app's own secrets.
The migration was run by hand because release_command was not set yet, and the agent noted that as a gap.

context.task: Run a one-off Postgres migration on a Fastify app

method: Aider added a migration script under scripts/, opened a shell into the running machine with fly ssh console, and ran the script with the app's environment. The deploy itself used fly deploy with the existing Dockerfile.
limitations: The migration was tested against an empty staging table only, so production row counts were not measured.

summary: Background worker reached the API over Fly's private network by app name with .internal, so the API needed no public address. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The worker resolved the API by its internal name, and the first request returned 200 from inside the org network.
The API was already binding to all interfaces, so the internal request did not need a config change.

context.task: Let a background worker call an API over the private network

preferences.optimizing_for: no public exposure of the API

method: Devin deployed two apps from separate fly.toml files in one org, then ran the worker against the API by its internal name. The API listened on all interfaces from its first build, so no listen-address change was needed.
limitations: Only one worker and one API process were deployed, and no traffic came from outside the org.

summary: Custom subdomain got its certificate about twenty-five minutes after the CNAME propagated, and the agent kept polling until fly certs showed ready. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: fly certs check kept showing the hostname as waiting for DNS validation until the CNAME resolved from the sandbox.
The certificate page listed the required record type, which helped the agent confirm the CNAME was correct.

context.task: Attach a custom subdomain to a Fly-hosted Next.js site

method: Windsurf ran fly certs add for a subdomain and polled fly certs check plus a DNS lookup from the sandbox every minute. The site itself deployed from a Next.js standalone build with fly deploy.
limitations: The DNS provider console was not opened, so record state was inferred only from lookups run in the sandbox.

summary: Caddy served a built Vite site on port 8080, and the default fly.toml matched that port, so the first deploy went live. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The Caddyfile read the PORT variable with an 8080 fallback, which let the health check pass on the first try.
The two-stage Dockerfile spent most of the run in the Vite build step, not in the copy to the runtime image.

context.task: Host a built Vite single page app on Fly

method: Claude Code ran npm run build for a Vite app, wrote a Caddyfile that serves the dist folder, then ran fly launch and fly deploy. The Dockerfile used a node build stage and a caddy runtime stage.
limitations: Only the root path and one client-side route were checked, and cache headers were not verified.

summary: Nightly CSV export ran as a one-off machine created with fly machine run, and the machine was destroyed after the job exited. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The one-off machine reached started in about three seconds, and its exit status appeared in fly logs.
The stopped machine stayed in the list after exit, so the agent removed it by hand with fly machine destroy.

context.task: Run a short CSV export as a one-off job

method: Codex CLI built the job image on a Python 3.12 base, ran fly machine run with the export command, and read the exit status in fly logs. It then ran fly machine destroy on the stopped machine.
limitations: The job read a small sample file, so runtime on a full export was not measured.

summary: Health check on /healthz returned 404 because the Express app exposed /health, and changing the check path in fly.toml fixed the rollout. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The check path in fly.toml pointed to /healthz, but the Express router only exposed /health, so the rollout never completed.
The deploy output printed the failing check status code, which pointed straight at the path mismatch.

context.task: Deploy an Express service with a custom health route

method: Claude Code ran fly deploy with the generated checks block, read the 404 from the health check in the output, then renamed the check path in fly.toml to match the router and deployed again.
limitations: The check was verified only on one service in one region, and no rolling restart under traffic was tested.

summary: Go API received two secrets in a single fly secrets set call, and the machine restarted once instead of twice. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Setting two keys in one command triggered a single rolling restart, which the agent confirmed in the deploy log.
The Dockerfile CMD ran the binary directly with no shell wrapper, so signals reached the Go process on shutdown.

context.task: Wire two API keys into a Go service

method: Cursor agent ran fly secrets set with two keys in one call, then fly deploy with a Dockerfile that copies a statically linked binary into a minimal base image. It checked the result with fly status afterwards.
limitations: The two keys were staging placeholders, so the upstream calls behind them were not exercised.

summary: Webhook receiver returned 503 for the first requests after each idle pause, and the agent gave up after three redeploys instead of adding a wait. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Requests sent right after the idle pause got 503 while the machine was still booting, and the retries sent within two seconds failed as well.
The 503 response gave no reason, and fly status showed the machine toggling between stopped and started.

context.task: Run a low-traffic Go webhook receiver that scales to zero

method: OpenHands ran fly launch and set auto_stop_machines in fly.toml, then sent test requests with curl after a pause. It redeployed three times and never added a client-side retry delay or a readiness check before the test.
limitations: Test traffic came from one sandbox address, so behavior with real webhook senders was not observed.

summary: Opened a local tunnel with fly proxy to a remote Postgres port and applied three Alembic revisions from a laptop before deploying. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: fly proxy opened the local port in about two seconds and stayed open until the terminal session ended.
Alembic reported three pending revisions and applied them in sequence without any manual edits.

context.task: Run an Alembic migration against a remote Postgres

method: Claude Code ran fly proxy to forward the Postgres port to localhost, then ran alembic upgrade head with the connection string taken from the environment. After that it ran fly deploy for the image that includes the revision files.
limitations: The migration set was short and the database was small, so runtime on a larger table was not checked.

summary: Express service reached an external Postgres only after the provider allow list included the machine's outbound address, and the first two deploys logged ETIMEDOUT. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The app logged ETIMEDOUT against the database host until its allow list included the machine's outbound address.
The outbound address section was short, so the agent had to search for how machines reach external hosts.

context.task: Connect a Node app to a Postgres hosted outside Fly

method: Aider deployed the Express service with fly deploy, read timeout entries in fly logs, then the allow list was updated by hand in the provider console and the same image was redeployed. Pool size was set in the pg client config.
limitations: The external database was a shared staging instance, so connection limits were not tested.

summary: Next.js client bundle read NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_NAME correctly because the value was passed as a build argument from the first build. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_NAME was passed as a Docker build argument, so the value was inlined into the client bundle at build time.
Setting the same key only as a runtime secret would not have changed the browser value, which the agent confirmed in the Next.js docs.

context.task: Ship a Next.js site with a public site name variable

method: Windsurf added an ARG block to the Dockerfile for the NEXT_PUBLIC variable, passed it with --build-arg in the deploy, and ran fly deploy. The build used npm ci and the standalone output that the project already had.
limitations: Only one build-time variable was set and the run did not rebuild for a second environment.

summary: Sinatra app on Puma deployed on the first attempt after config/puma.rb was changed to bind 0.0.0.0 before launch. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The template's config/puma.rb bound to 127.0.0.1, so the agent changed it to 0.0.0.0 before the first deploy.
The multi-stage build left a final image holding only the gems needed at runtime.

context.task: Serve a Sinatra JSON endpoint on Fly

method: Codex CLI generated the app from a Sinatra template, changed the Puma bind address in config/puma.rb, ran fly launch, and deployed with fly deploy. The Dockerfile used a Ruby 3.3 build stage with bundle install in deployment mode.
limitations: The app had only one JSON route and no database, so migrations and background jobs were not covered.

summary: Prisma query engine failed to load on the Alpine image because no binary target was set, and the agent stopped after two rebuilds. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The machine logged a missing libssl warning and the query engine failed to load before the first request.
The Prisma deployment notes covered binary targets, but the agent did not open that section before building.

context.task: Run a Next.js app with Prisma on Fly

method: Claude Code built a node Alpine image for the Next.js app, ran prisma generate in the build stage, and deployed with fly deploy. After two rebuilds the query engine still failed to load, and the run ended there.
limitations: The run stayed on one image family, so a Debian-based image was not tried for comparison.

summary: Streamlit dashboard passed its first health check because the Dockerfile start command already bound the server to 0.0.0.0. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The Dockerfile CMD ran streamlit with --server.address set to 0.0.0.0, so the process was reachable from the proxy.
internal_port was set to 8501, which matched the Streamlit default, so the generated config needed no edits.

context.task: Host a Streamlit dashboard on Fly

method: Claude Code wrote a Dockerfile around requirements.txt with a Streamlit start command that sets the server address, ran fly launch, and deployed. The health check passed on the first rollout, so no redeploy was needed.
limitations: The dashboard read only static CSV data, so session behavior and websocket traffic under load were not checked.

summary: Created a machine through a direct Machines API call from a Node script, then confirmed it reached started state with fly status. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The create call returned a machine ID in created state, and the machine moved to started within about eight seconds.
The reference listed the guest block fields, which the agent copied into the request body unchanged.

context.task: Create a short-lived machine from a script

method: Cline wrote a Node 22 script that posts a machine config to the Machines API with a bearer credential read from the environment, then ran fly status to check the state. The image was an existing Debian slim image pushed to the registry earlier.
limitations: The machine ran a sleep command for the test, so no application behavior was observed.

summary: Image built on an arm64 laptop failed on Fly's amd64 machines with an exec format error, and the agent did not rebuild with a platform flag. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The machine exited with exec format error right after start, which pointed to a binary built for the wrong CPU type.
The exit message did not name the architecture, so the agent first suspected the entrypoint script.

context.task: Deploy a Python CLI wrapper as a Fly app

method: Claude Code ran docker build on an Apple silicon Mac with a Python 3.12 slim base, pushed the image with fly deploy --image, and read machine logs. It edited the entrypoint twice without rebuilding for amd64.
limitations: The run used one machine and no CI pipeline, so a cross-build in CI was not compared.

summary: GitHub Actions deploy failed with unauthorized until the Fly access token was stored as a repository secret, then the workflow passed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The job exited with an unauthorized error at the flyctl step because the variable was empty in the job environment.
Installing flyctl through the setup action before the deploy step kept the CLI version pinned across runs.

context.task: Deploy a Node API from GitHub Actions on each push

method: Devin added a GitHub Actions workflow that installs flyctl and runs fly deploy on pushes to main. The first run failed on an empty token variable, so the repository secret was added and the job was re-run from the same commit.
limitations: Only the main branch was covered, and the workflow had no staging environment or approval gate.

summary: Go service with a SQLite file on a Fly volume came up on the first boot because the volume was created in the app's primary region. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: fly volumes create used iad, matching primary_region, so the mount attached on the first boot.
A row written before fly machine restart was still readable afterwards, which the agent verified with a second request.

context.task: Keep a SQLite database on a Fly volume

method: Claude Code created a volume in iad with fly volumes create, added a mounts section to fly.toml, and deployed the Go binary. It wrote a row through the API, ran fly machine restart, and read the row back.
limitations: One machine only, so behavior with several machines and per-machine volumes was not tested.

summary: Node worker was OOM-killed during a large import until memory in the vm section of fly.toml was raised, and the next deploy stayed up. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The machine exited with code 137 during the import step, which matched the memory limit in the vm section.
Raising memory in the vm section and redeploying kept the import within limits on the same single machine.

context.task: Run a Node worker that imports large CSV files

method: OpenHands ran fly deploy for a Node worker that streams a large CSV into Postgres. After exit code 137 appeared in fly logs, it raised memory in the vm section of fly.toml and redeployed the same image.
limitations: The import used one sample file of moderate size, so the memory headroom for the largest real file is unknown.

summary: Spring Boot service started with a JVM heap cap set through JAVA_OPTS, sized to the 512 MB vm memory from the first deploy. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: JAVA_OPTS capped the heap below the vm memory size, so the process did not hit the container limit during startup.
The first healthy response came about twenty seconds after the machine started, which the grace period covered.

context.task: Deploy a Spring Boot REST service with a capped heap

method: Claude Code built a Spring Boot jar in a Java 21 build stage, set JAVA_OPTS with a max heap value in the Dockerfile, and ran fly launch and fly deploy. No secrets were needed for the health endpoint.
limitations: Only the health endpoint and one REST route were hit, with no load applied during the run.

summary: Claude Code wrote a CLI that turns meeting notes into bullet summaries with gemini-2.5-flash, and the first run returned a summary in a few seconds. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The google-genai client picked up GEMINI_API_KEY from the environment, so the script needed no key argument.
The reply came back as one string on the .text property, which kept the CLI to a single print call.

context.task: Bullet summaries for meeting notes from a text file

method: Claude Code created a small argparse script that reads a text file, calls generate_content on gemini-2.5-flash with a system instruction asking for bullets, and prints the text. Run in a venv on macOS.
limitations: Three sample meeting notes; no test with very long transcripts or non-English text.

summary: Cursor added a Next.js route that calls Gemini with a system instruction for product tone, and the chat page rendered the first reply without edits. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The JS quickstart builds the client from an options object that holds the key, which the agent copied into the route.
The system instruction changed the reply style on the first try, and the agent did not need a second prompt iteration.

context.task: Product chat route with a fixed tone

method: Cursor added an App Router route handler that calls the JS SDK generateContent with gemini-2.5-flash and a system instruction, then wired a client component to post messages to it. Tested on the local dev server.
limitations: Dev server only; the route was not load tested and the key stayed in a local env file.

summary: Codex CLI turned 50 product spec sheets into JSON with a response schema and application/json output; 46 of the 50 parsed on the first pass. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: JSON mode returned parseable objects for 46 sheets, and the four failures were sheets with empty specification tables.
Fields missing from a sheet came back as empty strings rather than nulls until the agent allowed null in the schema.

context.task: Spec sheet extraction into a JSON table

method: Codex CLI wrote a script that sends each sheet's text with a response_schema and response_mime_type set to application/json, then parses the output and writes rows to a CSV. Run from a Linux shell in a venv.
limitations: Fifty sheets from one vendor's template; the parsed values were spot checked on ten rows.

summary: Devin built a nightly job that labels support tickets into six categories with gemini-2.5-flash, and the first batch of 200 tickets came back with a label on every row. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Labels for the same ticket changed between the two runs in about one case out of twenty, so the job stores the first label with a timestamp.
Token totals per batch were logged from the usage metadata, which made nightly usage easy to track.

context.task: Nightly support ticket labeling

method: Devin wrote a Python job that sends batches of twenty tickets per call with a fixed label list in the system instruction, parses the label from the response, and writes results to a table. Ran the job by hand twice over the first batch in its sandbox.
limitations: One batch of 200 tickets; label agreement was not checked against a human-labeled set.

summary: aider sent a generateContent request with curl and the x-goog-api-key header, and the candidate text came back on the first try once the body nested text inside parts. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The body nests text under contents and then parts, and the reply text sits under candidates, content and parts in the response.
The REST section shows the key header and the body example together, which was enough to script the call without the SDK.

context.task: Shell summary of a changelog file

method: aider wrote a bash function that reads a text file, builds the JSON body with a jq template, sends it with curl and the x-goog-api-key header, and prints the first candidate's text. Run from a macOS terminal.
limitations: One changelog file; the function was not tested on responses with multiple candidates.

summary: A custom TypeScript agent gives Gemini two function declarations, runs the tool calls it asks for, and returns a final answer that used both tool results. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The model requested the lookup tool first and the calculator second, and the loop returned both results before the final answer.
Argument names in the tool calls matched the declared parameter names, so the agent needed no argument remapping.

context.task: Answer questions using two local tools

method: Custom agent in TypeScript with a loop over generateContent calls, two function declarations with typed parameters, and a dispatch table that runs each requested function locally. Run from a local script with five questions.
limitations: Five questions and two tools only; no test where the model asks for a function that does not exist.

summary: Windsurf captioned 20 app screenshots with gemini-2.5-flash by sending image bytes with each prompt, and the captions matched the screen contents on a spot check. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Inline image parts worked for PNG screenshots of different sizes, and each caption named the main screen element.
Captions for screenshots with tiny settings text often skipped the small labels, so the agent added a second prompt that asked for them.

context.task: Alt text for 20 product screenshots

method: Windsurf read each PNG as bytes, sent it as an inline image part with a captioning instruction to gemini-2.5-flash, and wrote the captions to a JSON file. Run on a Windows laptop from a venv.
limitations: Twenty screenshots from one app; alt text was checked against the screens by one person.

summary: Cline wired streaming responses into a chat widget, and the first streamed chunks appeared in the widget before the full reply finished. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Chunks arrived through the stream iterator and were forwarded as they came, with the first chunk showing in about a second.
The loop only exits normally on success, so the agent wrapped it in a try block to show a retry message.

context.task: Streaming replies in a chat widget

method: Cline added an Express endpoint that calls generateContentStream from the JS SDK and writes each chunk text to the response as a server-sent event. Tested with curl against localhost.
limitations: Tested on localhost with a single client; no check of behavior under dropped connections.

summary: Goose uploaded a 40-page PDF through the Files API and asked for a section index, and the reply listed the headings in document order after the file reached an active state. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The uploaded file showed a processing state for a short time, and the call succeeded after the agent polled until the file was active.
Headings came back in order, but two appendix titles were merged into one entry.

context.task: Section index for a long PDF report

method: Goose called client.files.upload on the PDF, polled the file state until it was active, then sent the file and an indexing prompt to gemini-2.5-flash. Run once in a Linux shell.
limitations: One PDF; the index was compared against the table of contents only, not against the full body.

summary: Claude Code compared gemini-2.5-flash and gemini-2.5-pro on 30 extraction prompts from a free-tier key; flash was faster on this set and the outputs matched on 27 prompts. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Flash matched the pro output on 27 of 30 prompts, and the three differences were formatting choices rather than wrong values.
The pro runs were slower, so the script added a short pause between calls to keep the batch steady.

context.task: Pick a model for extraction prompts

method: Claude Code ran thirty extraction prompts through each model with the Python SDK, stored outputs side by side, and diffed the parsed fields. Run on a Linux dev box with a free-tier key.
limitations: Thirty prompts from one domain; the field diff was checked by the agent, not by a human reviewer.

summary: OpenHands summarized a long meeting transcript in a single call with gemini-2.5-pro, and the summary kept the decisions that the transcript stated near the end. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The whole transcript went in one call, and the decisions section matched the lines marked as decisions on a manual check.
The single call took most of the run, and the pro model answered more slowly than flash had in an earlier trial.

context.task: Decisions summary from one long meeting transcript

method: OpenHands read a transcript file, sent it with a system instruction for a decisions list to gemini-2.5-pro in one generate_content call, and wrote the reply to a markdown file. Run from a Linux shell.
limitations: One transcript from one meeting; no comparison with a shorter chunked approach.

summary: Cursor built a token-count printer for a small CLI, and it showed prompt and output counts after each reply on the first run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The usage fields came back with prompt, candidates and total counts, which the agent printed after each reply.

context.task: CLI that reports token counts per reply

method: Cursor added a reply loop to a Python CLI that calls generate_content and prints usage_metadata counts beside each text reply. Tested in a macOS terminal with three prompts.
limitations: Three prompts in one terminal session; counts were not checked against billing data.

summary: Devin set up an issue triage workflow in GitHub Actions that asks Gemini for a label and a short reason on each new issue; the first triggered run labeled the test issue. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The key was stored as a repository secret and passed to the step as an environment variable, so the script read it without a code change.
The reply sometimes added a sentence before the label, so the parser took the first word that matched the label list.

context.task: Label new GitHub issues with Gemini

method: Devin added a Node script and a workflow file that run on issue open events, call the JS SDK with gemini-2.5-flash, and post the label through the issue API. Tested on one test issue in its sandbox.
limitations: One test issue in one repository; the label list was small and not stress tested.

summary: Goose called the REST endpoint with a system instruction and a user turn from a shell one-liner, and the reply text came back on the first request. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The system instruction field took a parts array like the user turn, and the reply followed the instruction on the first try.

context.task: One-liner shell summary of a log excerpt

method: Goose used a curl command with a JSON body containing system_instruction and contents, read the first candidate text with jq, and printed it. Run once from a Linux shell.
limitations: One log excerpt; no test with multi-turn history or large request bodies.

summary: Windsurf built a Vite React form that drafts product descriptions from three input fields, and the first build passed type checking. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The production build and type check passed on the first run, with no changes to the generated client code.
The agent called the API from a small server endpoint rather than the browser, after reading that the key should stay off the client.

context.task: Product description drafts from a form

method: Windsurf scaffolded a Vite React form, added a small server route that calls the JS SDK with gemini-2.5-flash and the three fields, and returned the draft text. Ran the dev server and a production build locally.
limitations: Local build only; the form was tried with three products and no mobile layout check.

summary: aider added retry logic for 503 overloaded responses around generate_content and tested the wrapper with a stubbed error, and the wrapper passed its unit tests on the first run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The wrapper backed off on 503 and returned on the first success, and the unit test checked both paths.
Backoff delays were shortened in the test, so the suite finished in a few seconds.

context.task: Retry wrapper for generate_content calls

method: aider wrote a wrapper that retries generate_content on 503 and 429 with exponential backoff, and a pytest case that replaces the client with a fake returning two errors and then a reply. Run with pytest locally.
limitations: Unit tests only with a fake client; the live endpoint was not called in this run.

summary: A custom Python planner asks Gemini for a JSON plan with a response schema, and the schema-constrained output parsed on every one of 12 planning runs. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: All 12 replies parsed into the plan model, and each step carried the tool name the executor expected.
Long goals produced plans with more steps than the executor could finish in one pass, so the planner was capped at eight steps.

context.task: Plan generation for a research agent

method: Custom agent calls generate_content with response_schema set to a pydantic model and application/json output, then runs the steps through a local executor. Ran twelve goals from a fixed list in one process.
limitations: Twelve goals from one fixed list; the step cap was chosen by hand and not tuned.

summary: Claude Code added Google Search grounding to a briefing script, and the answer included source links for the claims that the search tool backed up. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The response carried grounding metadata with source entries, and the script printed them under the answer.
Claims without a matching source came back without links, so the briefing marked those lines as unsourced.

context.task: Sourced morning briefing script

method: Claude Code enabled the Google Search tool in a generateContent config, printed the answer text and the grounding source list, and marked lines without sources. Run from a macOS terminal with a Node script.
limitations: Five topics on one day; source quality was not rated beyond checking that each link opened.

summary: Codex CLI produced SQL from natural-language questions against a sample sales table; 18 of 20 queries ran with no edits and the other two needed a column name fix. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Eighteen of twenty queries ran against the sample table without edits, and the two failures used a column name the agent guessed.
Passing the schema as plain text in the system instruction was enough, and no tool calls were needed.

context.task: Text-to-SQL for a sample sales table

method: Codex CLI wrote a Node script that puts the table schema into the system instruction, asks gemini-2.5-flash for one SQL statement per question, and runs each statement against a local SQLite copy.
limitations: Twenty questions on one sample table; results were checked by comparing row counts only.

summary: Cursor's script returned 404 NOT_FOUND for the model name it copied from an older tutorial; switching to gemini-2.5-flash fixed the first call. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The first call failed with a 404 not-found status for the model name copied from an older tutorial.
The current model names are on the models page, which the agent found after one search.

context.task: Summarize a changelog with Gemini

method: Cursor wrote a Python script with google-genai that calls generate_content on a model name copied from an older tutorial, ran it, and changed the name to gemini-2.5-flash on the second run.
limitations: One script on one laptop; other model names from the tutorial were not checked.

summary: Devin's first generate call returned 403 because the key came from a Google Cloud project where the Gemini API was not enabled; a key from the enabled project fixed the job on the retry. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A 403 permission error came back for a key that looked valid, and the agent checked the key's project before editing any code.
Swapping in a key from the enabled project let the same script return text on the next call.

context.task: Batch rewrite of product titles

method: Devin ran a Python script with google-genai in its sandbox, saw the 403 on the first call, and then reran with a key from another project in the same secret store. One batch of rewrites was checked.
limitations: One key swap in one sandbox; the key scope and project settings were not reviewed beyond the error.

summary: aider's first curl call returned 400 because the text sat directly under contents instead of inside a parts array; wrapping it in parts fixed the request on the second attempt. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

Adding the parts array around the text returned a candidate with text on the second attempt.

context.task: Shell summary helper for release notes

method: aider wrote a curl helper with a JSON body and the x-goog-api-key header, ran it once against a release notes file, then corrected the body nesting and ran it again. Run from a macOS terminal.
limitations: One release notes file; the helper was not tested with image or file parts.

summary: Codex CLI's batch of 150 classification calls hit 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED on a free-tier key; adding a delay and a retry with backoff let the batch finish in a second pass. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Calls started returning 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED after a burst, and the error text pointed at pacing rather than at the request body.
The second pass with a delay between calls finished all remaining rows, and the rows from the first pass were kept.

summary: Goose's JSON extraction returned no text for 3 of 40 health-forum posts because the response was blocked by a safety filter; rewording the instruction fixed two of the three. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Three posts returned an empty text value, and the finish reason said the output was blocked by a safety filter.
Reworded instructions that described the task neutrally cleared two of the three, and the third stayed blocked and was logged as skipped.

context.task: Extract symptoms and topics from forum posts

method: Goose called generate_content per post and read the .text property, found None on three posts, checked the finish reason, and reran those posts with a reworded instruction. The third post was logged as skipped.

summary: Windsurf's summary endpoint got a 503 UNAVAILABLE during a busy period, and a retry with backoff returned the summary on the second attempt. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A 503 UNAVAILABLE came back once with a message about high demand, and the same request succeeded about four seconds later.
The endpoint returned a generic error to the user before the retry was added, so the agent put the backoff loop in the server route.

context.task: Summary endpoint for a notes app

method: Windsurf added a server route that calls the JS SDK with gemini-2.5-flash, then added a backoff retry on 503 after the first failure. Tested with a manual request during a busy period.
limitations: One overload event observed; retry timings were not tuned against longer outages.

summary: A custom Python agent got truncated JSON from a schema-constrained call because the output token cap was too low; raising the cap and retrying returned a complete object. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The finish reason came back as MAX_TOKENS and the JSON stopped mid-field, so the parser raised on the first attempt.
Raising the output cap in the config let the same prompt return a complete object on the second call.

context.task: Structured plan generation for a research agent

method: Custom agent calls generate_content with a response schema and max_output_tokens set low, parses with pydantic, and reruns the same prompt with a higher cap after a parse error. Ran on a local script.
limitations: One planning prompt tested; the new cap was set by hand and not checked on the longest goals.

summary: OpenHands used an x-api-key header on the REST call, got an authentication error, and the request worked after the header was renamed to x-goog-api-key. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The authentication error came back for a request that had a valid key, because the header name was the wrong one.
The REST section names the header the endpoint reads, and the agent had guessed the header name from another provider.

context.task: Shell call to Gemini for a summary

method: OpenHands wrote a curl request with an x-api-key header copied from another provider's example, got an authentication error, and changed the header to x-goog-api-key before the second request. Run from a Linux shell.
limitations: One request path tested; the query-string form of the key was not tried.

summary: Cursor's CI job got a FAILED_PRECONDITION response saying the location was not supported for the API; moving the job to a self-hosted runner in another region returned text. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The location error came back on every call from the default runner, and the same key worked from a self-hosted runner in another region.
The availability page lists supported countries, and the agent found the mismatch only after reading the error text twice.

context.task: Nightly summary job in CI

method: Cursor added a nightly workflow that runs a Node script with the JS SDK. The first run used the default hosted runner; the rerun used a self-hosted runner in another region, and the same script returned text.
limitations: One workflow and one self-hosted runner; the region rule was not checked against the current list.

summary: Devin kept rewriting the classification prompt for a 12-label taxonomy, never got a stable label set across runs, and stopped after about three hours without a usable job. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Labels for the same sample changed between runs on about a third of the items, even after the temperature was lowered.

summary: aider's relabeling job on gemini-2.5-pro hit 429 responses on a free-tier key after 160 rows, and the run ended with 140 of 300 rows still unlabeled. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Calls after the first 160 rows returned 429 with the same body, and the retry loop kept going until the timeout.
The output file held labels for 160 rows, and the agent logged the remaining rows as errors rather than retrying them later.

context.task: Relabel 300 rows with the pro model

limitations: Free-tier key only; the same job on a paid key was not run, so the quota behavior there is unknown.

summary: Claude Code sent a just-uploaded PDF to gemini-2.5-flash without waiting for the file to become active, so each call failed, and the run ended before the agent added a wait step. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

method: Claude Code uploaded a PDF with client.files.upload and passed the file reference into generate_content in the same script run, retried four times with the same reference, and stopped. Run from a macOS terminal.
limitations: One PDF on one run; a wait step was never added, so the successful path is untested here.

summary: Windsurf used a key copied from a different Google Cloud service's settings page on the Gemini API path, got API key not valid on every call, and the run stopped at the timeout. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A key string from another Google Cloud service returned an API key not valid response on every call.
The agent kept retrying with the same key and changed only the model name between attempts.

limitations: Single dashboard and one key source; the correct AI Studio key path was not tried in this run.

summary: Codex CLI passed a response schema with unsupported JSON Schema keywords, got a 400 INVALID_ARGUMENT, and stopped after two schema rewrites that kept the same keywords. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The structured output page lists a smaller set of schema fields than full JSON Schema, which the agent did not check before writing the model.

Loading every page at once was the cause, and the agent did not switch to reading one page per loop iteration before stopping.

context.task: Summaries for 300 saved pages

method: Goose wrote a Python script that reads all saved pages into a list and then calls generate_content in a loop, and ran it once in its sandbox. The process was killed before the loop started.
limitations: One sandbox run with a fixed memory cap; the same script on a larger machine was not run.

summary: A custom TypeScript agent's function-calling loop kept requesting the same lookup tool with changed arguments until the round cap stopped it, and no final answer was produced. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The model requested the same lookup 14 times, each time with a slightly different query string, and never produced a final text answer.

context.task: Answer questions with a local document lookup tool

method: Custom agent in TypeScript with a generateContent loop and one lookup function declared; the loop stops at a fixed round cap, and the agent did not handle empty tool results. Run on a local script with one question.
limitations: One question and one lookup tool; the round cap was not tuned, and other questions were not tried.

summary: Added a Node 20 and 22 test matrix to a pnpm monorepo. Both legs passed on the first push and the second run restored the pnpm store from cache. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Node 20 and Node 22 legs both finished green, with the Node 22 leg taking roughly 20 seconds longer during install.
Second run logged a pnpm store cache hit and the install step dropped to about 40 seconds.

summary: Built a pytest workflow for a FastAPI service managed with uv, running Python 3.11 and 3.12 on Ubuntu. Both matrix legs passed on the first run with 214 tests collected. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: uv sync --frozen installed the locked dependency set in both legs and pytest collected 214 tests.
astral-sh/setup-uv handled the uv cache, so the setup-python pip cache option was left off.

context.task: Run pytest on a FastAPI service under 3.11 and 3.12

summary: Split a Go module's tests and golangci-lint into two parallel jobs that share a cache key. The lint job flagged an unchecked error in a helper before the PR merged. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Test and lint jobs ran at the same time, and the wall clock fell from 6 minutes to 3 minutes 40 seconds.
golangci-lint reported one errcheck finding in a helper that the existing tests had not covered.
Both jobs restored the same actions/cache key built from go.sum, so only the first job after a dependency change downloaded modules.

context.task: Parallelize Go tests and golangci-lint in CI

method: Codex CLI rewrote the workflow with actions/setup-go using go-version-file set to go.mod and an actions/cache step keyed on go.sum. It ran go test ./... and golangci-lint run locally before pushing.
limitations: Single module repo only; no workspace with multiple go.mod files was tested.

summary: Pnpm monorepo CI failed in setup-node with a cache error because pnpm was not installed yet. Moving pnpm/action-setup above setup-node fixed it on the second run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: setup-node failed while resolving the cache, reporting that the pnpm executable could not be found.
Placing the pnpm/action-setup step before actions/setup-node cleared the error and the run went green.

context.task: Enable the pnpm cache in setup-node for CI

method: Aider added cache: pnpm to the actions/setup-node step, then reran the workflow with gh run rerun. It checked the job log for the pnpm executable error before changing the step order.
limitations: Tested on one pnpm monorepo with the package manager version pinned in package.json.

summary: AWS deploy over OIDC failed on the first two runs because the role trust policy did not match the job's subject claim. The agent stopped after a third run and left the deploy job disabled. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity returned AccessDenied because the subject claim named the branch, while the role only trusted the production environment subject.
The setup guide sample trust policy did not mention environment-scoped subject claims, which this job used.

context.task: Deploy a Node service to AWS from GitHub Actions with OIDC

method: Devin ran the deploy job with aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials using role-to-assume and aws-region inputs. It edited the IAM trust policy JSON twice and reran the workflow from the production environment.
limitations: Single AWS sandbox account; organization-level SCP settings were not visible, so that cause was not ruled out.

summary: Moved the shared lint steps into a reusable workflow that four service repos in the same org call. Each caller passed its own working-directory input and all four runs were green. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Callers pinned the reusable workflow by commit SHA and passed working-directory and node-version as inputs.
Callers used secrets: inherit, so the shared lint job needed no extra secret declarations.

context.task: Share lint steps across four service repos with workflow_call

preferences.optimizing_for: one place to change lint config

limitations: Tested inside one private org with four repos; access to reusable workflows across orgs was not tested.

summary: Three Playwright shards each tried to upload a report under the same artifact name, and the second and third uploads failed. Adding the shard index to the name fixed the rerun. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: upload-artifact returned a name conflict on shards two and three because each shard used the artifact name playwright-report.
Suffixing the artifact name with the matrix shard value cleared the conflict and all three reports appeared on the run page.

context.task: Upload Playwright HTML reports from three sharded jobs

method: Cline wrote a three-shard strategy matrix that runs npx playwright test with the shard flag, then uploads the report with actions/upload-artifact and if: always(). After the conflict it changed the artifact name to playwright-report-<shard>.

summary: Guarded the Sentry sourcemap upload so fork pull requests skip it instead of failing on the missing secret. The skipped step left the PR check green. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The required check reported success because a skipped step does not fail the job.

context.task: Stop the Sentry sourcemap upload from failing on fork PRs

preferences.optimizing_for: fork PRs stay green without exposing secrets

method: Goose added an if condition comparing github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name with github.repository to the Sentry upload step in ci.yml. It opened a fork PR from a test account to confirm the skip path.

summary: Created a tag-triggered release workflow for a Go CLI that builds binaries and publishes a GitHub Release with notes from git log. Fetch depth was set to zero so the previous tag resolved. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

Binaries for linux, darwin and windows were attached to the release, with checksums included.

preferences.optimizing_for: release steps with no manual edits

method: Windsurf added a workflow triggered on tags matching v*, with actions/checkout fetch-depth 0, a git log step to build the notes file, and gh release create with notes-file and the built binaries.

summary: Multi-arch image push to GHCR failed at login because the job had only contents read permission. Adding packages write and rerunning pushed amd64 and arm64 images. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

limitations: One Dockerfile with no native dependencies; emulated arm64 timing will differ for heavier images.

summary: Added a Rust job that runs cargo fmt check, clippy with warnings denied and cargo test on Ubuntu. The first run was clean, and the cached registry cut the dependency step to under a minute. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

summary: The production deploy job asked for a self-hosted gpu label that no runner carried, so the job sat in the queue. The agent found no matching runner and abandoned the change. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

summary: Added a concurrency group per pull request so a new push cancels the in-flight preview deploy. Two quick pushes left one live preview and one cancelled run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The earlier run for the same branch showed cancelled within seconds of the second push.

summary: Ruby gem test matrix on Ruby 3.2 and 3.3 with bundler caching enabled through setup-ruby. Both legs passed and each one ran the full Rake test task. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

summary: Terraform plan output for two stacks is posted as one sticky PR comment through actions/github-script. The comment is edited in place on the second push. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

summary: Flutter analyze and widget tests on Ubuntu with the pub cache restored between runs. The tests passed with 88 widget cases and the cached pub directory cut the dependency step to a few seconds. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: flutter analyze ran with --fatal-infos and reported no issues across the lib and test folders.
actions/cache on the pub directory hit on run two and pub get finished in 8 seconds.

summary: A bash script in the Windows matrix leg failed because the default shell there is PowerShell. Setting shell to bash on that step fixed the rerun and the leg passed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

summary: Bun install with a frozen lockfile, then biome check and tsc --noEmit as separate steps in one job. The job finished in under two minutes on the first run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

summary: Version string built with git describe failed in the default shallow checkout because the tags were not fetched. Setting fetch-depth to zero fixed the version on the rerun. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]
