Adding the run date as a property made the daily events countable without relying on the ingest time.

context.task: Send ad hoc test messages from a terminal command

method: Windsurf in a small TypeScript CLI repo. Added a send command with recipient and stream flags, a startup token check, and printed output. Ran it against a test mailbox on the transactional stream and once on a broadcast stream.
limitations: Single macOS laptop with one test mailbox; no CI usage or rate handling was added.

summary: SvelteKit form action sends a quote request copy to the sales test mailbox with the reply address set to the customer. Aider wrote the action, and the copy arrived with the customer address in Reply-To during a local run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Reply-To came from the validated form field, so replies from the sales inbox go to the customer directly.
Validation errors return to the form as a field message, and the send only runs after the input passes.
The server token is read through the SvelteKit private env module, which keeps it out of the client bundle.

context.task: Forward quote request copies from a SvelteKit form action

method: Aider in a SvelteKit project with a form action in the quote page. Added a server-only module that calls the email endpoint with the server token, validated the form fields, and sent one copy to the test mailbox.
limitations: One test mailbox and a single quote form; the sales team's real mailbox routing was not set up.

summary: FastAPI background task sends a password change notice with httpx and the server token, and the first run against a test mailbox returned a MessageID. The signup endpoint returns before the email call finishes. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: An httpx AsyncClient is created once in the lifespan hook and reused by the background task.
The background task runs after the response is returned, so the request handler does not wait on the email call.
Error responses are returned as JSON with ErrorCode and Message, and the task logs both before it gives up.

context.task: Send password change notices from a FastAPI background task

method: Custom SDK agent in a FastAPI project with shell and file tools. Added a lifespan hook for the async client and a background task that posts the notice, then ran the app and triggered one change against a test mailbox.
limitations: One test mailbox and a local uvicorn process; the background task was not tested under concurrent requests.

summary: Node route got a 401 on its first send because the account token was used in place of the server token, and the route returned a MessageID after the header was switched. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The 401 body carried ErrorCode 10 and a message about a bad or missing token, which pointed at the header value rather than the payload.
The value in the environment was an account token copied from the wrong settings page, so the server header received the wrong credential.
Swapping in the token from the server settings let the next send return a MessageID with no other change.

context.task: Send a receipt email from a Node route
context.blocker: account token used as server token

method: Claude Code in a Node service. Wrote a send helper with the server token header from env, triggered it from curl, read the 401 body, then compared the stored value against the server tokens list and re-ran the request.
limitations: One service and one test mailbox; the other servers in the account were not compared against this token.

summary: Sender address on a newly added domain was rejected until a person approved it from the check mail Postmark sends to that address, and the next send returned a MessageID. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The error said the sender signature was not confirmed and named the From address rather than the domain.
The agent could not open the mail for that address, so a person approved the sender from it.
The second send after approval returned a MessageID, and the retry was the only change between the two requests.

context.task: Send a test message from a newly added sender address

method: Cline in a Node script on a macOS laptop. Sent one test message from an address that had just been added as a sender, read the error body, then re-sent after a person approved the address from the mail Postmark delivered.
limitations: Single sender address on one account; domain-level verification was not part of this run.

summary: Sends from a freshly verified domain failed with a verification error while the DKIM check was still pending, and the same send passed about forty minutes later. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The DKIM status stayed pending after the TXT record was added, and the dashboard did not explain the delay.
Querying the TXT record with dig showed the value at the authoritative server before the local resolver had it.
The same request went through on the next attempt once the status changed, with no change to the payload.

context.task: Send from a newly verified sending domain

method: Devin in a sandbox with a DNS record list handed over by a person. Read the record back with dig, sent one test message through the REST endpoint, then polled the domain status every few minutes and sent again once it changed.
limitations: One domain and one DNS provider; timing reflects this propagation window and will differ elsewhere.

summary: Transactional template call returned an error about a missing template because the alias in code did not match the lowercase alias on the template list. The copied alias rendered the welcome note on the next call. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The alias in code had a capital letter that the template list shows in lowercase, and the lookup returned an error for it.
Copying the alias from the template list page, rather than from memory, removed the mismatch.

context.task: Send a welcome note through a template alias

method: Cursor in a Node script that calls the withTemplate endpoint. Ran the script with an alias typed from memory, read the error, then copied the alias from the template list and reran the same model.
limitations: One template with two variables; the template body was not reviewed beyond the rendered subject.

summary: Attachment in the quarterly export arrived unreadable because the file was base64 encoded twice, and the re-send after removing one encode step opened correctly. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The attachment helper encoded the bytes in a utility and again in the send call, so the payload was base64 of base64.
The first message delivered, but the PDF would not open in the test mailbox, which counted as one failed run.
Removing the second encode and re-sending produced a readable PDF in the test mailbox.

context.task: Send a quarterly export PDF as an attachment

method: Aider in a Python job. Read the export PDF, encoded it in a helper, and encoded it again inside the send call. Opened the received message, found the file unreadable, removed the extra encode and re-sent.
limitations: One PDF of a few pages sent to one test mailbox; larger files and other mail clients were not checked.

summary: Batch of forty messages came back with two entries flagged as inactive recipients, which the agent traced to addresses that had bounced earlier, and the rerun without them completed the rest. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The batch response listed one result per message, with error details on two entries and MessageIDs on the other thirty eight.
Both failed addresses had earlier bounces on the account, so the API refused them as inactive recipients.
Filtering those two addresses and re-posting the remaining entries completed the batch with no new errors.

context.task: Send a forty message batch of update notices

method: Goose in a Python script that reads a JSON list and posts it to the batch endpoint in one request. Read the per-message results, excluded the two failed addresses, and posted the rest again. Test addresses only.
limitations: Forty test addresses with two seeded bounces; suppression rules on a live list may behave differently.

summary: Webhook handler rejected every Postmark event with a 401 because the basic auth password in the webhook URL did not match the one in the route, and the events were accepted once the values were aligned. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Every event returned 401 because the username and password in the configured URL did not match the values the route expected.
Replaying a saved Delivery event after the fix passed the auth check and updated the matching row.
The route logs the auth header length rather than its value, so the mismatch was found without exposing credentials.

context.task: Accept Postmark delivery webhooks behind basic auth

method: Windsurf in a Next.js route handler. Added basic auth parsing, a length-only debug log for the header, and a switch on RecordType. Triggered three test events from a saved payload and aligned the credentials in the route with the URL.
limitations: Single webhook endpoint with saved payloads; the production URL was not updated during this run.

summary: Loop sending weekly digests to a test list of two hundred addresses hit 429 responses after a fast start, and a backoff with jitter let the remaining sends finish on the second pass. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A burst of sends returned 429 after the first few dozen calls, and the loop kept going without pausing.
A backoff with jitter on each 429 let the second pass finish with no further throttling responses.
Chunking the list into groups of twenty with a short pause kept the first pass under the throttle.

context.task: Send weekly digests to a test list of two hundred addresses

method: OpenHands in a Python loop over a CSV of test addresses. First pass sent without pauses and hit 429 responses, then added chunks of twenty, a short pause, and jittered backoff. Reran the failed rows on a second pass.
limitations: Two hundred test addresses on one account; throttle behavior at production list sizes was not measured.

summary: Template send was rejected because the request named a broadcast message stream, and the send passed after the stream name was switched to the transactional one. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The API refused the request with an error naming the stream, and the agent had copied the value from an older example.
Checking the stream list in the account showed the transactional stream under its default name, which the code then used.
The second request returned a MessageID, and the activity view listed it under the transactional stream.

context.task: Send a template message from a REST call

method: Devin in a sandbox with a Node script that posts a template model to the withTemplate endpoint. Ran the script once with a stream name copied from an old example, read the error, then pulled the stream list from the account and reran.
limitations: One account and one template; other streams on the account were not reviewed beyond the default list.

summary: Staging run used the test server token, and every send returned a MessageID, but nothing reached the test mailbox. The agent reported success until a person checked the inbox and the run was marked failed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The test token returns IDs and timestamps that look real, so the response shape gave no sign that nothing was sent.
The empty test mailbox was only noticed after a person looked, because the agent never read the activity view.
The agent did not compare the token value with the staging config before the first send.

context.task: Verify staging sends reach a test mailbox

method: Claude Code in a Node service with a staging env file. Sent five test messages through the email endpoint, read the returned MessageIDs, and marked the run complete without opening the test mailbox.
limitations: Staging environment only; the live server token was never loaded, so delivery behavior on that token is not covered.

summary: New account sends to addresses outside the team were refused until the account was approved, and the agent stopped after three attempts without a path to test delivery. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The first sends to outside addresses returned an error about the account not yet being approved for that recipient.
Each retry used the same recipient and payload, so the three attempts produced the same error.
The approval request lives in the provider's own account flow, which the agent could not open from the sandbox.

context.task: Send a first real notice from a new Postmark account
context.blocker: account not yet approved for sending

method: OpenHands in a sandboxed VM with a Python script that posts one notice to an outside address. Ran it three times with the same payload and read the error body each time, then stopped at the approval message.
limitations: One new account in a sandbox; the approval timeline and the result after approval were not observed.

summary: Postmark delivery webhook pointed at a preview deployment that sat behind deployment protection, so the events were answered by the gate and the run was abandoned after the webhook test failed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Requests from outside were answered by the protection gate, so the handler never ran for the test events.
Test deliveries from the provider side reported failures, but the agent could only see its own local replays.
The agent did not switch the preview to a public URL or add a bypass header, so the endpoint stayed behind the gate.

context.task: Receive Postmark delivery webhooks on a preview deployment

method: Custom SDK agent in a Next.js project deployed to a Vercel preview. Added a webhook route, replayed saved events locally, and tried to trigger provider test deliveries against the preview URL. Stopped after the fourth try.
limitations: Single preview URL on one project; production deployments and other protection settings were not checked.

summary: Rendered welcome emails showed blank names for every recipient because the model keys were camel case and the template expected snake case, and the agent could not find an error to fix. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Missing template variables render as empty strings, so the API returned success with blank greetings.
The model used firstName while the template body read first_name, and nothing in the response flagged the difference.
The agent read the template twice and the model once without spotting the key mismatch, and the run stopped there.

context.task: Fix blank names in welcome emails from a template

method: Cline in a Node service that renders a template through the withTemplate endpoint. Sent three test messages with a model built from a database row, compared the rendered output with the template, and stopped when no error appeared.
limitations: One template and three sample rows; the fault may differ in templates with nested model objects.

summary: Domain verification for a new sending domain stayed incomplete because the Return-Path CNAME was created with the CDN proxy on, and the agent ended the run before the record was switched to DNS only. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The Return-Path record was created as a proxied entry, so the lookup returned proxy addresses instead of the expected target.
The domain status stayed pending across eight checks spaced about five minutes apart.
The agent had read-only access to the DNS provider, so the proxy setting had to be changed by a person.

context.task: Verify a Postmark sending domain behind a CDN proxy

method: Codex CLI on macOS with a read-only DNS API token. Looked up the Return-Path record and the DKIM record, checked the domain status on repeated polls, and stopped after eight checks when the record was still proxied.
limitations: One DNS provider and one domain; the result depends on how that provider handles proxied CNAME entries.

summary: Inbound webhook handler sent each message to a chat notifier before returning, took about forty seconds on large messages, and the agent stopped after the timing runs without moving the work to a background job. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The handler waits on the chat notifier before responding, so the webhook request stays open for the whole notifier call.
Messages with long HTML bodies took about forty seconds in the test, and the logs showed most of the time spent in the notifier.
The agent did not move the notifier into a background job, so the request time stayed the same after two edits.

context.task: Process inbound forwarded messages with a chat notifier

method: OpenHands in an Express service with an inbound webhook route. Added a call to a chat notifier inside the handler, sent sample inbound payloads with curl, and timed the responses. Made two edits to the handler and stopped after the third timing run.
limitations: Synthetic inbound payloads of two sizes; real mailbox traffic and the notifier's own latency were not measured.

summary: Rails app was set to send over SMTP from a sandbox whose outbound port was closed, so every delivery attempt timed out and the run was abandoned before the HTTP API path was tried. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Each delivery attempt waited until the connection timed out, and the error never reached the mailer code as an API response.
A raw socket check to the SMTP host from the sandbox failed, which showed the outbound port was blocked.

context.task: Send a notice from a Rails app inside a sandbox

method: Custom SDK agent in a Rails repo with a sandbox shell. Set the mailer to SMTP settings from the Postmark docs, ran a test delivery with bin/rails runner, and checked the socket from the sandbox after each timeout. Stopped after the fifth attempt.
limitations: Single sandbox with no outbound SMTP access; the same settings were not run on a host with open ports.

summary: Scaffolded an inbound-mail Function with the primitive CLI and deployed it to a managed inbox. The first deploy went through, and a test email to the inbox reached the handler log within a minute. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The scaffold command created a handler file with the inbound message shape and a deploy script, so the agent edited only the reply logic.
The Function stayed silent until a route was bound with the fallback flag, which the agent only added after reading the CLI help text.

context.task: Deploy a Function that answers inbound support mail

method: Claude Code in an empty project folder. Ran the CLI scaffold for an inbound Function, edited the handler to read the sender and subject, deployed it, bound the fallback route, and sent a test message from a personal mailbox.
limitations: Used one managed inbox on the Developer plan; no custom domain was attached and mail volume was a handful of test messages.

summary: Python script sent a daily status note through the SDK and passed an Idempotency-Key built from the date. The first run delivered the message, and a rerun the same day returned the original send without a duplicate. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Passing a key derived from the date made the second call return the first message id, which the agent verified in the sent list.
The script printed the message id on success and exited non-zero otherwise, which kept a failed send visible in the cron log.

context.task: Send a daily status note from a cron job

method: Aider in a small Python repo. Wrote one send function that sets the Idempotency-Key header from the date and a fixed label, ran it twice in one day, and compared the returned message ids.
limitations: Tested the same-day rerun only; keys across days and behavior when the content changes between runs were not checked.

summary: Agent tried to send a first outbound message from a new account to an external address and got a 403 with recipient_not_allowed. The run switched to replying inside an inbound thread, which the account permitted. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The 403 with recipient_not_allowed came back on the first send, and the error body pointed to the account state rather than the address.
Replying to a message that arrived through the inbox went out without the same error, so the reply flow worked during the test.

context.task: Send the first outbound email from a fresh inbox

method: Cline in a Node 22 project using the official SDK package. Called the send method for a new address, read the 403 body, then sent a reply to a message from a test sender through the thread id.
limitations: Only a freshly created account was tested; the timeline for enabling outbound sends on that account was not observed.

summary: Agent set up a custom sending domain and waited on DNS verification from a sandboxed container. The records were published correctly, but the sandbox resolver could not reach public DNS, so the status never moved to verified. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The status check kept returning pending while the agent's lookups timed out, which looked like a record error until the timeouts were traced.
The CLI listed the SPF, DKIM and DMARC entries with their names, which made it easy to compare against the registrar screen.

context.task: Verify a custom domain for outbound mail

method: Devin in a sandboxed Linux shell with the primitive CLI installed. Added the listed records through the registrar API, then polled the domain status and ran dig against the record names from inside the sandbox.
limitations: The sandbox resolver could not reach public DNS, so verification was never reached and the propagation time was not measured.

summary: Express service verified Primitive webhook signatures before handling message events. The first replay passed the check on the raw body, and a second replay with a tampered body was rejected with the expected status. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The verifier needed the untouched request bytes, so the route was placed before the JSON parser and used a raw body reader.
The timestamp check rejected a delivery older than the window, and the agent confirmed the window by sending an old-dated event.

context.task: Accept inbound message webhooks securely

method: Claude Code in an Express 4 service on Node 22. Mounted the webhook route before express.json, verified each request with the SDK helper, and replayed a valid and a tampered delivery from a local script.
limitations: Tested with local replays only; the production secret and its rotation were not part of this run.

summary: Webhook subscription was created with an event type spelled message.received in one place and message.recieved in another. The second spelling matched no events, so the agent's test delivery never reached the handler. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Unknown event type names are accepted without error, so the typo produced a subscription that silently matched nothing.
Listing the subscription showed the stored event type, and comparing it to the handler's case branch exposed the difference.

context.task: Subscribe a handler to inbound message events

method: Codex CLI in a Node service with a webhook handler. Created the subscription through the CLI, triggered a test delivery, saw no log line, then compared the stored event names with the handler's switch statement.
limitations: Checked one event type with a typo; the set of accepted event names and how the platform validates them later was not explored.

summary: Go program sent a reply inside an existing thread and attached the thread id from the inbound payload. The reply landed under the original conversation on the first run, with the subject carried over unchanged. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The reply call took the message id of the inbound mail, and the outgoing message reused the thread without a separate subject argument.
The client constructor read the key from the environment, and the agent kept it out of the source file.

context.task: Reply in-thread to inbound support mail

method: A custom SDK agent in a Go service. Read the inbound message id from the webhook body, called the reply method with the thread context, and checked the stored thread in the inbox listing after one test message.
limitations: Replied to one test thread with a single recipient; multi-recipient threads and attachments were not included.

summary: Agent gave up on a Function that never received mail. The deployed handler was healthy, but no route was bound to the inbox, and after thirty minutes of retesting the run ended with the mail still unrouted. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The deploy command reported success, and nothing in its output said that a route was still missing for the inbox.
The logs stayed empty because no message ever reached the Function, which made the handler look broken to the agent.

context.task: Route inbound mail to a deployed Function

method: Claude Code in a Function project deployed with the CLI. Rewrote the handler twice and redeployed, sent test messages from two mailboxes, and read the Function logs after each send without binding a route.
limitations: The agent never ran the route command, so the run shows the silent-failure pattern only and not a working inbound setup.

summary: Function stored a conversation state value in the Memories key-value store between inbound messages. The second message from the same sender read the saved value, and the reply referenced the first request correctly. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A read after a write from the same handler returned the stored value, which let the reply pick up the earlier request without a database.
Keys were built from the sender address, and the agent lowercased the address first so case differences did not split one conversation.

context.task: Keep context across a two-message support thread

method: Windsurf in a Function project. Wrote the handler to save the last request under a key built from the sender, sent two messages from one mailbox, and checked the reply text for the earlier detail.
limitations: Only two messages from one sender were tested; key growth and cleanup over many conversations were not measured.

summary: Support Function gated a refund-request action on the sender's trust status and ignored the From header text. A spoofed display name was tested and the action stayed blocked, which the agent logged for review. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The check used the trusted sender flag from the inbound payload, so a matching display name with a different address did not pass.
The test message with a copied display name was rejected by the gate, and the log line recorded the sender address instead.

context.task: Restrict privileged actions to trusted senders

method: Claude Code in a Function handler using the Node SDK package. Added a guard on isTrustedSender before the refund branch, then sent a spoofed message and a trusted message from two mailboxes to compare the outcomes.
limitations: Two sender mailboxes were used for the spoof test; the guard was not reviewed against other header forgery paths.

summary: Cursor edited a Next.js route so that a contact form sends a notification through the SDK. The first send in the browser went out with the right sender name and reached the test inbox within a minute. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The send call sat in a server route, and the key was read from the server environment rather than the client bundle.
The form's reply-to field was passed as the thread reference only when present, so an empty field did not break the send.

context.task: Send a notification email from a contact form

method: Cursor in a Next.js App Router project. Added a POST route that validates the form fields, calls the send method with a fixed sender address on a managed inbox, and tested with the local dev server.
limitations: Used the default managed inbox address; a custom sender domain and its verification were not part of this run.

summary: Install of the package on Node 20 failed with an engine error, and the agent upgraded the runtime to Node 22 before the second install worked. The rest of the scaffold ran without changes. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The npx run stopped with an unsupported engine message on the old runtime, so the agent switched the shell to a Node 22 install.
After the upgrade the scaffold command produced the same handler and deploy files that the docs describe.

context.task: Install the CLI and scaffold a Function

method: Goose on a Linux machine with Node 20 preinstalled. Ran npx for the scaffold, read the engine error, installed Node 22 through nvm, and reran the scaffold in an empty folder.
limitations: Only one fresh Linux image was used; macOS and Windows installs with Node 20 were not tried in this run.

summary: Devin tried to replay inbound messages against the hosted Function from a sandbox. Requests to the platform were refused at the sandbox boundary, so no message was delivered and the run ended in the first hour. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The CLI reported a connection failure before any authentication step, which the agent first read as a bad key.

context.task: Test a hosted Function with inbound replays

method: Devin in a sandboxed shell with the primitive CLI installed. Set the account key from the environment, ran the login check and a message send, then retried the same commands with a verbose flag to read the connection error.
limitations: The sandbox blocked outbound connections, so the hosted path was never exercised and no delivery behavior was observed.

summary: Replayed a set of failed webhook deliveries from the CLI after the handler was fixed. The replay sent each stored event once, and the handler returned 200 for all of them on the first pass. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The replay command took the failed delivery ids from the listing, so the agent did not need to copy payloads by hand.
Each failed delivery had already been retried by the platform, and the handler dedupes on the event id, so the manual replay did not double process.

context.task: Recover missed webhook deliveries after a handler bug

method: Claude Code in a Node webhook service. Listed the failed deliveries for the test inbox, replayed them with the CLI after the fix, and checked the handler log for one line per event id.
limitations: Replayed five failed deliveries from a test inbox; the platform's retry schedule was not timed against production traffic.

summary: Function reading a rotated secret kept using the old value after an update, and the agent saw auth failures until the Function was redeployed. The second deploy picked up the new secret and the test send succeeded. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Updating the secret did not reach the running Function, and the logs showed the stale value until a fresh deploy replaced the instance.
The redeploy command was one line, and the agent added it to the runbook so the rotation step was not skipped again.

context.task: Rotate the outbound API secret used by a Function

method: OpenHands in a Function project with the CLI. Updated the stored secret, sent a test message to see the auth error, then redeployed the Function and sent another message to confirm the new value was used.
limitations: Only one secret was rotated in a test project; rotation under live mail flow and overlapping secrets were not tested.

summary: Checked a custom domain from a local shell after the records were set at the registrar. The CLI status changed to verified on the third poll, about ten minutes after the last record was added. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The status stayed pending for several minutes after the records resolved locally, then changed to verified without any change on the agent's side.
The record names in the status output matched the zone file exactly, which removed the need to compare them by hand.

context.task: Verify a custom sending domain

method: Aider with a shell script that polls the domain status command every minute. Added the three records at the registrar, confirmed each one resolved from the local resolver with dig, and let the status poll run until it changed.
limitations: Verification was checked on one domain from a single local resolver; other registrars and their propagation times were not compared.

summary: Codex CLI tested the idempotency header with two sends that had different keys and identical content. Both messages went out, and the content-based dedupe did not apply because the keys differed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A send with a new key and the same body as an earlier send was delivered again, which confirmed that the key takes priority in the test.
Sending the same body without any key inside the five minute window returned the earlier message id, so the agent added keys to every send path.

context.task: Confirm send deduplication rules before a retry wrapper

method: Codex CLI in a Node service with a send wrapper. Ran three sends in a row with and without Idempotency-Key, read the returned message ids, and changed the wrapper so every call sets a key.
limitations: Three sends were compared in a test inbox; behavior after the five minute window and under concurrent sends was not measured.

summary: Function parsed a PDF attachment from an inbound message, and the process was killed when the parser loaded the whole file into memory. The run stopped after the first large attachment without a usable reply. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The Function's memory ceiling of 128 MiB was hit by a fifteen megabyte PDF once the parser expanded the page images.
A two page PDF processed in the same Function without trouble, so the failure was tied to file size rather than the code path.

context.task: Summarize PDF attachments from inbound mail

method: Claude Code in a Function handler using a pure JavaScript PDF parser. Sent a two page test PDF and then a fifteen megabyte scanned PDF, and read the Function logs for the memory error.
limitations: Only one large scanned file was used; streaming parsers and chunked reads were not tried, so a fix is unverified.

summary: Python script listed the last day of inbound messages with the SDK and printed sender and subject for each one. The listing returned the test messages in order, and the script exited cleanly on an empty page. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Messages came back newest first, so the agent reversed the list before printing the day's sequence.
The cursor was returned on each page, and the empty final page ended the loop without a separate count call.

context.task: Print a daily digest of inbound mail

method: A custom SDK agent in a Python script. Called the list endpoint for the last twenty four hours, followed the cursor until it was empty, and printed a table of sender and subject values.
limitations: Listed a dozen test messages in one inbox; the paging behavior for large inboxes was not measured in this run.

summary: Python retry wrapper around the send call derived its key from the draft id. A timeout on the first attempt was followed by a second call that returned the original message id, and the wrapper logged it as a replay. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The second attempt after a simulated timeout returned the first message id, so the wrapper reported success without sending a duplicate.
The wrapper had no field for replays, so the log line looked like a new send until the agent compared message ids.

context.task: Send an approval note safely after a network timeout

method: Aider in a Python service. Wrapped the send method with a retry loop, forced a client timeout after the first call, derived the Idempotency-Key from the draft id, and compared the message ids from both attempts.
limitations: The timeout was forced in the client; server-side slowdowns and the five minute dedupe edge were not exercised.

summary: Deployed an Express JSON API with railway up, and the app read PORT from the environment on the first try. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The first deploy answered on the generated public address once the app read PORT from the environment.
The build used the Node setup it detected from package.json, and no Dockerfile was needed.

context.task: Deploy the web app from a pnpm monorepo
context.blocker: root directory points at wrong package

method: Windsurf created a web service for the web app, set the root directory to apps/api by mistake, and edited the build command three times. It did not revisit the root directory, so the deploys kept building the API package.
limitations: Only one monorepo layout was tried, so other workspace layouts were not compared.

summary: Vite single page app deployed as a static site, and a rewrite rule sent deep links back to index.html. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Without the rewrite rule, a deep link returned a 404 from the static host, and with it the route rendered.
The publish directory was set to dist, and the static build finished in under a minute.

context.task: Host a Vite single page app as a static site

method: Claude Code created a static site from the repo with npm run build as the build command and dist as the publish directory. It added a rewrite rule that routes all paths to index.html and tested a deep link after the first publish.
limitations: Only the client-side routes in the sample app were tested, and no cache headers were checked.

summary: Scale-out to two instances failed on a service with a persistent disk, and the agent stopped without trying a single-instance layout. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The scale request was refused for the service with a disk attached, which the error text tied to the single-instance rule.
The disks page described the single-instance limit, but the agent read it only after the refused call.

context.task: Run a Node service with a disk in two instances

method: Codex CLI attached a persistent disk to a paid web service through the REST API and then requested two instances. After the refused call it retried the same request twice and stopped.
limitations: The run used one web service in one region and did not try a shared storage service.

summary: Phoenix app connected to Render Postgres with the internal database URL, and the release task ran before the server started. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The release command ran the Ecto migration before the server started and printed the migration output to the deploy log.
The internal URL worked from the web service without any IP allow list change.

context.task: Connect a Phoenix app to Render Postgres

method: Claude Code added a release script that runs the Ecto migration, set the start command to the release entry point, and linked the database from the Render dashboard. It deployed from the main branch and checked the logs for the migration output.
limitations: The schema change was additive, and the run did not include a rollback.

summary: Go service built from a Dockerfile with a multi-stage build, and Render used the Dockerfile path set in the service settings. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The Dockerfile path was set to docker/Dockerfile in the service settings, and the build picked it up without a rename.
The final image held only the compiled binary and CA certificates, and the layer pull was quick.

context.task: Ship a Go binary from a Dockerfile

method: Cline wrote a two-stage Dockerfile that compiles a static Go binary and copies it into a scratch-based final stage with CA certificates. It set the Dockerfile path in the service settings and deployed from main.
limitations: The service had one HTTP route and no outbound calls were tested.

summary: Custom domain showed an unverified state because the CNAME target had a typo, and the agent fixed the record on the second attempt. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The domain stayed unverified after the first check, because the DNS record pointed at a target with a missing dash.
Re-checking after the record fix moved the domain to verified, and the certificate was issued within a few minutes.

context.task: Attach a custom domain to a Render web service

method: Cursor agent added the custom domain in the service settings, copied the CNAME target into the DNS zone, and polled the verification status. After noticing the target did not match the dashboard, it corrected the record and waited for verification.
limitations: One subdomain on one provider was tested, so apex domain handling was not covered.

summary: Pull request preview environment came up for a branch with its own database, and the preview served the branch build. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The preview spun up for the pull request branch and served the branch build without any manual steps.
The preview used a separate Postgres instance, so writes from the branch did not reach the main database.

context.task: Set up preview environments for pull requests

method: Devin enabled pull request previews on the blueprint, added a preview database to render.yaml, and opened a pull request with a small UI change. It checked the preview build log and loaded the page after the preview finished.
limitations: Only one pull request was opened, and preview cleanup after merge was not observed.

summary: Docker build failed because the Dockerfile skipped copying the prisma folder, and the second build passed after the COPY line was added. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The build stage failed on prisma generate because the schema file was not copied into the image.
The second build reused the dependency layer, so the rebuild took about a minute.

context.task: Build a Next.js app with Prisma from a Dockerfile

method: Claude Code ran the Docker build on Render from the repo Dockerfile, read the prisma generate failure, and added a COPY line for the prisma folder. It redeployed from the same commit with the Dockerfile change.
limitations: The app had a small schema, so generate time for a large schema was not measured.

summary: Created a Render web service from a script with the REST API, then read its deploy status until the first build finished. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The create call returned the service ID in the response, and the deploy status moved to live after the build finished.
The reference listed the required fields for a web service, and the agent copied the example body without changes.

context.task: Create a web service from a script

method: Cline wrote a Node 22 script that posts a web service definition to the REST API with an account credential from the environment, then polls the deploy list until the status is live. The repo and branch were passed as fields in the request body.
limitations: The run created one service in a test workspace, so bulk creation and rate limits were not tested.

summary: Webhook sender timed out on the first request after an idle gap, and the retry landed after the free instance woke up. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The first request after the idle gap took long enough that the sender's timeout fired, and the retry was served normally.
The sender's built-in retry succeeded on the second attempt, and the test event was stored once.

context.task: Receive webhooks on a free web service

method: Aider deployed a Flask webhook receiver to a free web service and sent a test event after twenty idle minutes. It read the sender log and confirmed that the retry reached the app after the instance was awake.
limitations: One sender and one test event were used, so behavior under a real webhook burst was not measured.

summary: Upload handler wrote user files to a persistent disk mounted at /var/data, and the files were still there after a manual restart. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The disk attached at /var/data before the first boot, and the uploader wrote to that path without a permission error.
A manual restart kept the uploaded files in place, which the agent checked with a directory listing.

context.task: Store uploads on a persistent disk

method: Claude Code added a disk at /var/data in the service settings, changed the upload directory to read from an environment variable, and deployed. It uploaded two test files, ran a manual restart, and listed the directory afterwards.
limitations: Two small files were uploaded, so disk sizing and growth were not measured.

summary: Service crash-looped at boot because a shared environment group was never attached, and the agent kept editing the code instead. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The crash log showed a KeyError for the shared API base value, which lived in an environment group the service was not linked to.
The agent edited the config loader three times and never opened the service's environment tab.

context.task: Boot a TypeScript API that reads shared settings from an environment group

method: Cursor agent created a web service from the repo and read the crash logs after each restart. It rewrote the config loader three times and redeployed each time, but never linked the environment group to the service.
limitations: The run covered one service, and the environment group contained only three variables.

summary: Auto-deploy was limited to the main branch, so a push to a feature branch left the live service on the last main build. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Pushes to a feature branch did not start a deploy, and the live service kept the last main build.
Merging the branch into main triggered one deploy, and the commit hash in the deploy list matched the merge commit.

context.task: Auto-deploy a Next.js site from GitHub main

method: OpenHands set the auto-deploy branch to main in the service settings, pushed a feature branch, and then merged it. It compared the deploy list entry with the merge commit after the build finished.
limitations: Only one feature branch and one merge were tested, and no pull request previews were enabled.

summary: Build failed an engines check until NODE_VERSION was set to the version in package.json, and the second deploy passed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: npm refused to install because the engines field asked for a newer Node than the build image provided.
Setting NODE_VERSION in the environment tab fixed the build on the next deploy without other changes.

context.task: Deploy a Node 22 service with an engines constraint

method: Codex CLI created a web service with npm ci as the build command and node dist/server.js as the start command. After the engines error it set NODE_VERSION to 22 in the environment tab and redeployed.
limitations: One service on a single region, and only the production build was tested.

summary: Service account JSON was loaded from a Render secret file, so the credential never entered the repo or the build image. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The secret file mounted at its configured path before the process started, and the app read it on boot.
The build log had no copy of the file contents, because the secret file was added after the build step.

context.task: Load a service account file for a Node worker

method: Claude Code uploaded the service account JSON as a secret file in the service settings, pointed the app's credential path at the mount location, and deployed from main. It confirmed the file was readable after boot with a one-line check in the logs.
limitations: The file was used only for a single read-only API call, so long-lived credential rotation was not tested.

summary: Local analytics tool connected to Render Postgres through the external database URL after its IP address was added to the allow list. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The external URL connected from the laptop once the laptop's public address was on the database allow list.
The allow list accepted a single address entry, and the agent added it in the database settings page.

context.task: Query Render Postgres from a local analytics tool

method: Windsurf looked up the laptop's public address, added it to the database allow list, and connected with the external URL from a local env file. It ran a read-only count query to confirm the connection.
limitations: One read-only query was run, and the allow list entry was not tested after the laptop's address changed.

summary: Headless Chromium was killed during a page render on the paid instance, and the agent kept increasing timeouts instead of memory. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The process exited with an out-of-memory signal during the third page render, and the instance restarted.
Raising the navigation timeout did not change the exit, because the restarts came from memory pressure.

context.task: Run a Playwright scraper on a Render web service

method: Devin deployed a Playwright scraper as a web service with a Chromium install in the build step, and it ran a batch of pages through a single browser. It raised the navigation timeout twice and reopened the batch without changing the instance size or the number of tabs.
limitations: Only one batch of pages was run, and the instance size was never changed during the run.

summary: Health check on /api/health got a 401 because the route sat behind auth middleware, and moving the check to a public route fixed the rollout. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The health check received a 401 because the route was registered after the auth middleware, so every deploy failed its check.
Registering a public health route before the middleware let the next deploy pass without other changes.

context.task: Deploy a Node API with an auth-protected router

preferences.optimizing_for: no auth bypass for other routes

method: Claude Code deployed the API with /api/health as the health check path, read the 401 in the deploy log, then moved the health route above the auth middleware and redeployed. It left every other route behind the middleware.
limitations: Only the health route and one protected route were checked after the fix.

summary: Web service reached a private worker service through its internal service name and port, and the private call returned on the first try. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The web service called the private service by its internal name and port, and the call returned within a few milliseconds.
The private service had no public address, so only the web service reached it during the test.

context.task: Let a web service call a private worker over the internal network

preferences.optimizing_for: no public endpoint for the worker

method: Codex CLI created a private service for the worker and a web service that calls it by the internal name on the configured port. The worker listened on 0.0.0.0 in its listen call, and the web service sent one test request.
limitations: One test request was sent and the worker did not run any long jobs during the check.

summary: Cron job failed twice on a relative script path, and the third run passed after the command used an absolute path. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The job's command used a relative path, and the working directory in the cron runner did not match the repo root, so the file was not found.
The run history showed the error code for each failed run, which made the path issue easy to find.

context.task: Run a Python cleanup script as a cron job

method: Aider set the cron command to python scripts/cleanup.py, triggered two manual runs, and read the run history. It changed the command to an absolute path under the app directory and triggered a third run that completed.
limitations: Only manual triggers were used, so the scheduled run path was not checked separately.

summary: Frontend on another host got a CORS error from the API on Render, and allowing the frontend origin in the server config fixed it. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The browser console showed a CORS error on the preflight request, because the API allowed only its own origin.
Adding the frontend origin to the allowed list in the server config cleared the error on the next deploy.

context.task: Call a Render API from a separately hosted frontend

method: OpenHands deployed the API and a static frontend as separate services and ran the frontend fetch from the browser. After the preflight failure it added the frontend origin to the CORS config, redeployed the API, and reloaded the page.
limitations: One frontend origin and one browser were tested, and credentialed requests were not checked.

summary: Two services read the same environment group, so a single change to the shared API base updated both on the next deploy. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Both services were linked to the same environment group, and the agent confirmed the shared value in each service's environment tab.
The group value change needed a manual redeploy on each service before the running process picked it up.

context.task: Share one API base value across two services

method: Claude Code created an environment group with the shared API base value through the REST API, then linked it to both services. It triggered a deploy on each service and compared the value printed at startup.
limitations: Only one shared value was used, and the two services were in the same region.

summary: Dockerfile path set to docker/worker.Dockerfile, with a Docker command override, ran the worker entry file on the first deploy. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The Docker command override replaced the image's default command, and the worker started with the expected arguments.
The Dockerfile path field accepted a nested path, so the repo kept one Dockerfile per service.

context.task: Run a second Dockerfile for a background worker

method: Cline added docker/worker.Dockerfile next to the web Dockerfile, set the Dockerfile path and the Docker command in the worker's settings, and deployed from main. It read the first worker log line to confirm the arguments.
limitations: The worker processed no real jobs, so only the startup path was exercised.

summary: Spring Boot service on the free plan passed its first health check, and startup finished well inside the wait window. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Startup took about twenty seconds, which fit inside the wait window without any change to the health check settings.
The JVM heap stayed below the free instance's limit under the test requests, and no restart was logged.

context.task: Deploy a Spring Boot REST service on the free plan

method: Codex CLI built a Java 21 jar in the Render build step with Maven, started it with java -jar and a capped heap, and used the free web service with the default health check. It sent a short burst of test requests and read the memory line in the logs.
limitations: The test burst was short, so memory behavior under sustained traffic was not measured.

summary: Go worker consumes a queue message and sends a receipt through the Go client with a five second deadline. Codex CLI added the deadline, and the first live send returned an id within the same run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A context with a five second deadline stopped a stalled HTTP call from holding up the queue consumer.
The returned value carried an id field, which the worker wrote to its job log before acking the message.

context.task: Send a receipt email from a Go queue worker

method: Codex CLI in a Go module with a worker main package. Added a sender package on top of the Go SDK, wired it into the consumer loop, and ran the worker locally against one queued test message before deploying a staging app.
limitations: Staging app only; the production secret was not loaded and the receipt template was plain text.

summary: Laravel controller sends a magic sign-in link through the PHP client after the email form posts. Cursor added a throttle to the route, and the link arrived in the test inbox during the first browser run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The signed URL was built with a fifteen minute expiry, and the mail body quoted that window in plain text.
The throttle middleware on the POST route blocked repeat sends from one address during the manual test.
Composer pulled in the client with no extra packages, and the constructor read the key through the framework config helper.

context.task: Send magic sign-in links from a Laravel controller

method: Cursor in a Laravel app. Created a controller and a mailable, pointed the send call at the PHP client, and posted the sign-in form from a local browser. Checked the route log and the provider dashboard for the send record.
limitations: Used one local browser and one test address, so the throttle values were not tuned against real traffic.

summary: Rails mailer for team invitations uses the Ruby client and an ActiveJob queue. Aider generated the mailer and job, and the invite arrived after the worker picked it up in development. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The mail was enqueued instead of sent inline, so the controller returned before the API call finished.
The mailer preview page rendered the invite template without any network call, which made the layout check quick.
The job logged the returned id and relied on the default job retry policy, with no custom rescue block added.

context.task: Send team invitation emails from a Rails mailer

method: Aider in a Rails app. Added an invitation mailer, a deliver-later job, and a mailer preview, then ran the job in development and read the id from the log line.
limitations: Development only, with the test queue adapter, so retry behavior under a real worker process was not exercised.

summary: FastAPI route forwards contact form messages to the team inbox through the Python client. Goose wired the endpoint, and the first submission reached the shared inbox with reply-to set to the visitor address. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Setting the reply-to field to the visitor address let the team answer from their own mail client without copying anything.
A length limit on the message field was added to the Pydantic model, and the send helper only runs for messages under that limit.
The route was declared async while the send helper blocks, which the timing log showed as a 200 ms stall until the call moved to a thread pool.

context.task: Forward contact form messages to the team inbox

method: Goose in a FastAPI service. Added a POST route with a Pydantic request model, called the Python SDK through a helper, and posted sample messages with curl against a local uvicorn process.
limitations: Local uvicorn with sample payloads only; the Render service was not deployed during this run.

summary: Cloudflare Worker sends a waitlist welcome over the REST endpoint with fetch, and the key is stored as a Worker secret. Cline ran it under wrangler, and the first request returned a message id. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: fetch is built into the Worker runtime, so no SDK package was added and the bundle stayed small.
The key came from a binding set with wrangler, and a missing binding threw a readable error at request time.
Non-2xx responses were passed back to the caller with their status code, which would make a bad sender visible in the browser console.

context.task: Send waitlist welcome emails from a Cloudflare Worker

method: Cline in a Worker project with wrangler. Wrote a fetch handler that posts JSON to the REST send endpoint with a bearer header, stored the key as a Worker secret, and tested with wrangler dev plus one curl request.
limitations: Ran under wrangler dev only; the deployed Worker on a custom route was not exercised in this run.

summary: Nitro server route in a Nuxt app sends the weekly changelog to twelve internal addresses with the Node client. Claude Code ran the route once against the test list, and every send returned an id. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Each recipient got its own call in a loop, and the route returned the ids as a list with a count.
The changelog markdown was converted to HTML before sending, so the body had headings and no raw markup.
The dev server read the key from runtime config, which Nuxt fills from environment variables at boot.

context.task: Send a weekly changelog digest from a Nuxt server route

method: Claude Code in a Nuxt project with Nitro server routes. Added a route that reads a changelog markdown file, converts it with a small parser, and sends one message per recipient through the Node SDK. Ran it on the dev server with a twelve address list file.
limitations: Dev server only and internal addresses, so the per-recipient loop was not measured under load.

summary: Nightly cron on a VPS posts the backup status report through the REST endpoint, with the body assembled by jq. Codex CLI added the script and crontab entry, and the first manual run delivered the report to the ops test address before the schedule was enabled. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: jq encoded the log tail as a JSON string, so newlines and quotes in the log did not break the request body.
Cron runs with a minimal PATH, so the script calls curl by full path and reads the key from a root-only file.

context.task: Post a nightly backup status report with curl from cron

method: Codex CLI on a small Ubuntu VPS. Wrote a shell script that builds the JSON body with jq, posts it to the REST send endpoint with curl, and checks the response id. Added a crontab entry and ran the script once by hand before enabling it.
limitations: One VPS and one ops recipient; no retry on network failure was added in this run.

summary: Deno Deploy function emails a numeric sign-in code through the REST endpoint for a small internal tool. Cursor wrote the handler, and the code arrived in the test inbox on the first local invocation. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Deno.env.get returned the key from project settings, and the handler failed fast when the value was empty.
The code came from crypto.getRandomValues and was stored in Deno KV with a five minute expiry.

context.task: Email a sign-in code from a Deno Deploy function

method: Cursor in a Deno project. Wrote a handler that generates the code, saves it in Deno KV, and posts to the REST send endpoint with fetch. Invoked the function locally with deno task and checked the response body.
limitations: Local invocation only, so the Deno Deploy runtime and its region were not part of the run.

summary: Phoenix context module sends export-ready notices through the Elixir client after a background task finishes. Claude Code added the module, and the first notice reached the requester's test address during a local run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The send ran under a Task.Supervisor, so a failed request logged an error instead of crashing the caller.
The key was read at runtime from release config, which kept it out of the compiled artifacts.
The export link was escaped before it went into the template, so query characters survived intact.

context.task: Send export-ready notices from a Phoenix background task

method: Claude Code in a Phoenix app. Added a context module with one send function, called it from a task under a supervisor after the export job completes, and ran the export locally in dev.
limitations: Local dev run with one export file; release builds and node restart behavior were not exercised.

summary: Spring Boot scheduled job sends account expiry reminders through the REST endpoint with RestClient. OpenHands wrote the job, and the reminder for one test account arrived after the scheduler fired. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The cron expression fires at the top of the hour in server time, which the agent confirmed with a one-minute test schedule.
Jackson serialized the request record with snake_case names, and the endpoint accepted them without a custom mapper.
The bearer header sits on a shared RestClient bean, so every call inherits it and no per-call header code exists.

context.task: Send account expiry reminders from a Spring Boot scheduler

method: OpenHands in a Maven project. Created a scheduled component, a RestClient bean with the bearer header, and a request record. Ran the scheduler with a one-minute cron against a test account and checked the logs for the returned id.
limitations: One test account and a one-minute schedule; the production cron expression and time zone were not reviewed.

summary: ASP.NET minimal API endpoint sends a booking reminder through the .NET client and returns the message id to its caller. Devin ran the endpoint in its sandbox, and the reminder reached the test address on the first pass. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Registering the client in the built-in DI container meant the endpoint and the background service shared one instance.
The endpoint returned 202 with the message id, so the caller could log the id without reading the body twice.
Only the account owner address accepted messages from the default sender, so the test used that address as the recipient.

context.task: Send booking reminders from an ASP.NET minimal API

method: Devin in a sandboxed VM with the repo cloned. Added a POST endpoint, registered the client in the DI container, and ran the app with dotnet run. Sent one request with curl and read the message id from the response body.
limitations: Sandbox run with one recipient; the reminder template was plain text and scheduled sending was not tested.

summary: Astro API route sends a double opt-in link for newsletter signups over REST. Codex CLI wrote the route, and the verification email landed in the test inbox with the link intact. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The verify URL is built from the site origin variable, so preview and production links point at their own hosts.
A hidden honeypot field was added to the form, and submissions that filled it were dropped before any send call.
On failure the route returns a generic message and logs the raw API text on the server side.

context.task: Send double opt-in links for newsletter signups from an Astro route

method: Codex CLI in an Astro project with a server endpoint. Added a POST route that validates the email, writes a pending row to a local JSON file, sends the verify link through fetch to the REST endpoint, and returns a generic message.
limitations: Pending rows live in a local JSON file during the run; no database writes and no unsubscribe flow were built.

summary: Hono route on Bun sends a support ticket acknowledgement with the Node client and puts the ticket number at the start of the subject line. Claude Code ran it under bun run, and the acknowledgement arrived on the first request. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The Node client loaded under Bun without a shim, and the send call resolved on the first try.
The ticket number sits at the start of the subject so replies stay grouped in the recipient's mail client.

context.task: Send ticket acknowledgements from a Hono route on Bun

method: Claude Code in a small Hono project run with bun. Added a POST route that takes a ticket number and a reply address, calls the Node SDK, and returns the message id. Tested with a bun run script that posts one sample ticket.
limitations: One sample ticket on a laptop; Bun's production image and cold start time were not measured.

summary: Small Node CLI sends release notes to a distribution list and prints the returned ids as a table. Windsurf added a dry-run flag, and the live run reached the list on the first try. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The dry-run path prints the rendered recipients without calling the API, which made repeating the list check safe.
A recipients file with trailing blank lines produced empty to fields until the parser trimmed each line.
console.table printed the ids in a layout the team could paste straight into the release thread.

context.task: Send release notes to a distribution list from a Node CLI

method: Windsurf in a CLI repo that uses commander. Added a send command, a dry-run option, and a file reader for recipients. Ran the dry run first, then the live send to a list of eight internal addresses.
limitations: Eight internal addresses on one macOS laptop; no CI runner or concurrent sends were involved.

summary: Django signup view sends a verification link through the Python client after the user row is saved. Windsurf wired the view, and the link in the first test email opened the account page locally. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The send happens after the transaction commits, so the link never points at a user row that is still rolled back.
The template takes the site domain from settings, and the agent checked the href in the rendered HTML.
The response id is written to the audit log with the user id instead of the email address, to keep addresses out of logs.

context.task: Send email verification links from a Django signup view

method: Windsurf in a Django project. Added a signup view that saves the user, then calls a helper that posts the message through the Python SDK. Ran the dev server, submitted the form, and opened the link from the test message.
limitations: Dev server and one test address; link expiry was left as a follow-up item in the run notes.

summary: Python script attaches a monthly usage PDF encoded as base64 and posts it through the REST endpoint. Goose handled the encoding, and the attachment arrived intact on the first local run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Reading the PDF in binary mode and encoding it once produced a body the endpoint accepted without changes.
The filename was set explicitly, so the recipient's mail client showed a readable name instead of a temp path.
The script exits non-zero on any non-2xx response, so the scheduler marks the run as failed.

context.task: Send a monthly usage PDF as an attachment from a Python job

method: Goose in a Python repo with a Lambda handler. Built the PDF in a temp file, read it as bytes, base64 encoded it into the attachments list, and posted through the REST endpoint. Invoked the handler locally with a sample event.
limitations: One small generated PDF was attached; attachment size limits and multi-file sends were not tried.

summary: Next.js server action emails a comment reply notice after a form submit, with the React email renderer running on the server. Cursor wired the action, and the first browser test reached the test address. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Keeping the render and send calls inside the server action kept the email package out of the client bundle.
The action returns an error string to the form on failure, which the UI shows under the submit button.
The notice link uses a base URL variable the agent added, so preview deploys point at their own hosts.

context.task: Email comment reply notices from a Next.js server action

method: Cursor in a Next.js app with a server action on the comments page. Imported the email component and the Node SDK only in the server file, rendered the notice, and submitted a reply in the browser to trigger a send.
limitations: Local dev server and one preview deploy; production traffic and inbox placement were not checked.

summary: Rust axum handler posts a quote summary through the REST endpoint using reqwest and serde structs. The custom agent ran cargo test on the mapping function, and one manual request returned a message id. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Serde skips the optional reply_to field when it is empty, so the API never receives an empty string for it.
The reqwest client is built once at startup and shared through axum state, instead of one client per request.

summary: Go service retried a PaymentIntent create after a 429 response and then sent a duplicate charge attempt. The idempotency key was generated per call, which was the cause. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A new uuid was generated inside the retry loop, so each attempt looked like a fresh request to the API.
The 429 responses carried a retry hint that the client code did not read, so the backoff was a fixed 200 ms.
The stripe-go error value exposed the request id and the decline code, which made the failure easy to log.

context.task: Retry a PaymentIntent create during a burst of checkouts

method: Aider on a small Go service with a retry wrapper around the charge call. Ran a load script against test mode with 40 concurrent requests and read the logged request ids.
