Fees arrived as minor units with a type field, which the notebook grouped and then divided once for display.

context.task: Reconcile monthly fees from balance transactions

method: OpenHands in a Jupyter notebook with the stripe Python package. Listed balance transactions for one test-mode month with auto_paging_iter, grouped by type, and compared the sums to the exported monthly report.
limitations: Ran against a small test-mode dataset; a large live account and its page sizes were not tested.

summary: Go service tried to create a Connect payout to a bank account in a country the test account could not send to. The payout call failed on every attempt, and the agent stopped after reading the country list. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The payout create call returned a country restriction error, and the account's allowed countries were only visible in the dashboard settings.

context.task: Pay out a connected account to a local bank

method: Claude Code in a Go service using stripe-go. Created a test connected account and attempted a bank payout in the country set on the account, then read the error code and the returned field list.
limitations: Only one connected test account in one country was tried, and the run did not look at onboarding requirements for other regions.

summary: Astro static page generated a Payment Link at build time and embedded it as a plain anchor. The build step needed the key only in CI, and the page shipped with no client JavaScript for checkout. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The build script created the link once per deploy, which meant a new link object on each rebuild; the agent added a lookup to reuse the existing one.
The generated HTML contained only the anchor and no key, which the agent confirmed by grepping the built output.

context.task: Link a product page to hosted checkout from a static site

method: Claude Code in an Astro 5 project. Added a build-time script that creates or reuses a payment link for each product price, then ran the build and inspected the output HTML for leaked keys.
limitations: Only static pages with fixed prices were built; no dynamic quantities or customer-specific links were generated.

summary: Celery worker retrieved a PaymentIntent before marking an order paid, instead of trusting the task payload. The retrieve call caught a payment that was still processing, and the task re-queued itself. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A retrieve right after confirmation returned processing for a bank debit, so the task checked status in a loop with a short sleep.
Passing only the intent id in the Celery message kept the payload small and avoided stale status values.

context.task: Mark orders paid from an asynchronous worker

method: Aider in a Python worker repo. Changed the task to accept an intent id, retrieved the intent, and re-queued with a countdown while the status stayed processing. Tested with a test-mode bank debit.
limitations: Only one delayed payment method was tried in test mode; real settlement times for bank debits were not measured.

summary: Node command-line tool listed every customer created in a month with auto paging and wrote them to a CSV file. The run covered about two thousand records and finished without any manual cursor code. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The for await loop over customers.list pulled pages on demand, and the memory use stayed flat compared with the first attempt that collected everything in an array.
The created filter expects unix seconds, and the first version passed milliseconds, which returned an empty list for the month.

context.task: Export customers created in one month

method: Goose in a small Node CLI. Wrote a script that takes a month argument, converts it to unix seconds for the created filter, iterates customers with for await, and appends rows to a CSV.
limitations: Exported a test-mode dataset of about two thousand customers; the run did not include a live account of comparable size.

summary: Next.js route looked up a customer with the search endpoint right after creating it, and the search returned no results for about a minute. A retry after a short wait found the customer. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Search results lag behind writes, so a customer created moments earlier was missing from the query until the index caught up.
Querying the customer by the stored id returned the object at once, which the agent used as the primary path.

context.task: Find an existing customer by email during signup

method: Claude Code in a Next.js app. Created a customer during a test signup, queried customers.search by email immediately afterward, and then switched the lookup to the stored customer id.
limitations: Measured the lag on one test account; the typical indexing delay under other loads was not sampled.

summary: Sidekiq job created invoice items for usage records at the end of each billing period. The first run charged a customer twice because the job had no idempotency key, and the retry path posted the same item again. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Sidekiq retried the job after a timeout, and the second run created another invoice item with the same description and amount.
Passing a key built from the customer id and period end stopped the duplicate in the test run.

context.task: Bill usage at the end of each period

method: Codex CLI in a Rails app with Sidekiq. Added a job that builds a deterministic idempotency key, forced a retry by raising after the first call, and checked that the second call returned the original item.
limitations: Only one usage type was billed in the test; idempotency key expiry and long period gaps were not tested.

summary: Flask app's 3D Secure step ran in a headless browser inside the sandbox to confirm the challenge. The browser could not reach the challenge host, so the run stopped at the redirect with no confirmation. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The payment intent stayed in requires_action because the challenge page never loaded, and the agent had no way to complete it in that environment.
The client code called handleNextAction as documented, but there was no browser session to receive the redirect back.

context.task: Complete a 3D Secure test payment end to end

method: OpenHands in a Flask app inside a sandbox with a headless browser. Created a test card intent that requires authentication, opened the client page, and waited for the return URL to fire.
limitations: The sandbox blocked the challenge host, so the 3D Secure screens were never seen and the flow is untested here.

summary: Go Lambda handler created a charge with a request-scoped context and a short timeout. The default HTTP client had no timeout set, so the first cold start hung until the function limit and the agent set one explicitly. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The SDK used the default client, and a stalled connection held the Lambda until it hit its own limit with no error from the SDK.
Passing a context with a five second deadline made the call return a context deadline error that the handler logged cleanly.

context.task: Charge customers from a serverless function

method: Claude Code in a Go Lambda project using stripe-go. Built a handler that takes the amount from the event, creates a payment intent with a five second context deadline, and deployed to a test stage in one region.
limitations: Tested in one AWS region with a test account; the timeout value was not tuned against real traffic.

summary: Python script moved a subscription to a new plan at the end of the current period using a subscription schedule. The first attempt updated the price immediately, so the agent rebuilt it with a phase boundary. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The schedule needed two phases, the current one and the next, before the new price applied at the boundary.
Switching to schedule phases removed the mid-period proration line that the immediate update had produced.

context.task: Downgrade a plan at the end of the billing cycle

method: A custom SDK agent wrote a script that converts an active subscription into a schedule and adds phases for the current and next period. Ran it on a test subscription and read the upcoming invoice.
limitations: Tested with one monthly test subscription; annual plans and trial-to-paid transitions were not included.

summary: React Native checkout sheet was added to an Expo app and tested on an iOS simulator. The payment sheet presented on the first run, and the agent wired the success callback to close the modal. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The sheet opened with the merchant display name from the init call, and the simulator run completed a test card payment.
A config plugin entry was required in app config before the native module linked, and the agent added it before the first build.

context.task: Add a native payment sheet to a mobile checkout

method: Claude Code in an Expo managed project. Added the native Stripe plugin to app config, fetched a payment intent from a test endpoint, and presented the payment sheet on an iOS simulator.
limitations: Only the iOS simulator was tested; Android and physical device flows were not run in this session.

summary: Vercel cron route summed yesterday's invoices by filtering on created timestamps in local time. The totals were off by a day for customers in a timezone ahead of UTC, and the agent switched the bounds to UTC. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The route computed midnight in the server timezone and passed it as the created lower bound, which excluded invoices from the early hours.
Listing invoices with the gte and lt bounds returned the expected count once the bounds were UTC seconds.

context.task: Compute daily invoice totals on a cron schedule

method: Claude Code in a Next.js route run by a Vercel cron. Listed invoices for a test-mode account with created bounds computed from local dates, then compared the totals with a manual count by UTC day.
limitations: Only one timezone offset was simulated; the run did not check daylight saving transitions or a live invoice export.

summary: Node service set max network retries on the client after a flaky VPN dropped connections during a batch of charges. Two calls hit transient errors before the retry count was raised and the batch finished. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Raising maxNetworkRetries from the default to three covered the dropped connections without changing the call sites.
The connection error arrived as a generic network error, and the logs did not show which attempt produced the final failure.

context.task: Run a batch of test charges over an unstable network

method: Cline in a Node batch script. Set the client's network retry option, ran twenty test charges through a VPN that drops packets, and counted the attempts logged for each charge.
limitations: A single VPN path was used to induce drops; other network conditions and their retry behavior were not compared.

summary: FastAPI checkout endpoint created a session with the customer email prefilled from the signed-in user. The session returned a hosted page address on the first request and the redirect worked in the browser. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Passing customer_email on the session created a field prefilled on the hosted page, and the agent skipped creating a customer object.
The success_url needed the session id placeholder, which the agent appended after the first attempt dropped it.

context.task: Start hosted checkout for a signed-in user

method: Codex CLI in a FastAPI app. Added a POST route that reads the user from the session, creates a checkout session with customer_email and a success_url placeholder, and redirects. Tested with a logged-in test user.
limitations: Only the default payment methods were enabled; the signed-in flow was tested with one user account in the browser.

summary: Rails initializer set the global API key and a pinned version for a new billing module. The agent found an older initializer that overrode the key with a stale value from a previous environment. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Two initializers both assigned Stripe.api_key, and the later file in load order won, which masked the change in the new one.
Setting Stripe.api_version in one place kept responses consistent across the controllers that the agent touched.

context.task: Centralize Stripe client configuration in a Rails app

method: Windsurf in a Rails 7 app. Searched the repo for every assignment of the Stripe key, removed the duplicate initializer, and moved the version pin into the one remaining config file with a test that reads it back.
limitations: Only the test environment configuration was checked; production initializer order was not loaded in this run.

summary: Express webhook route acknowledged events with a 200 right after verification and pushed the payload to a local queue. The agent confirmed that a slow handler no longer caused the Stripe retry loop to fire. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The old handler ran the database writes before responding, and a two second write delay pushed the response past the delivery timeout.
Enqueuing the verified event before responding kept the handler under a few milliseconds in the local test.

context.task: Keep webhook responses fast under slow writes

method: Claude Code in an Express service with a Redis-backed queue. Moved the write into a worker, responded 200 after enqueue, and replayed a burst of signed events with the Stripe CLI.
limitations: Queue durability and worker crash recovery were not tested; the run covered only the happy path on one machine.

summary: Batch refund script hit a read timeout after the refund was created on the server. Reissuing the call with the same idempotency key returned the original refund rather than a second one. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The second request returned the refund object with the same id, which the script logged as a replay instead of a new refund.
The key was derived from the order id, so the rerun after a crash matched the first attempt without any state file.

context.task: Refund a list of orders safely after a network failure

method: Aider in a Python script. Forced a client timeout after the refund request by wrapping the call, then reran the same order with the key built from the order id and compared the refund ids.
limitations: The forced timeout was simulated in the client; real server-side delays and key expiry windows were not tested.

summary: Next.js middleware on the Edge runtime tried to import the Node SDK to check a subscription flag. The build failed on the first deploy because the package depends on Node-only modules. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The bundle step rejected the import of a Node built-in module from inside middleware, and the error pointed at the stripe package path.
The agent moved the check into a route handler on the Node runtime, but the rewrite was not completed before the run ended.

method: Claude Code worked inside a Next.js app folder. Imported the Stripe client inside middleware.ts to read a subscription status cookie, ran the production build, and read the bundler output for the failing import.
limitations: Only the build output was checked; the deployed middleware never ran, so the runtime behavior after a fix is unknown.

summary: Spring Boot webhook controller read the signature header and the raw body, then verified the event with the endpoint secret. The first two attempts failed on a body that the servlet filter had already re-encoded. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A servlet filter that rewrapped the request changed whitespace in the JSON, so the signature check failed until the filter was excluded for that path.
After verification, the Event.construct result gave typed access to the payment intent, which the handler used without casting.

context.task: Process payment succeeded events in a Java service

limitations: Verified one event type locally; the production endpoint secret rotation procedure was not exercised.

summary: Go checkout service stored the order id in metadata and then looked it up through the search endpoint at confirmation time. The lookup worked, and the agent kept the metadata key short to stay within the limits. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

Loading the script from the footer delayed the form, so the plugin enqueued it in the head instead.

method: Claude Code in a WordPress plugin directory. Enqueued the Stripe script, rendered a mount point, and tested in a local browser session where the managed host's CSP header was not present.

summary: Deno Deploy function imported the Stripe npm package through the npm specifier and created a test payment intent. The handler ran on the first deploy, and the agent noted the import map entry it had to add. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The function responded with the intent id on the first request, and the deploy log showed no warnings about Node built-ins.

The route returned the answer string and results array unchanged, which kept the frontend contract simple.

context.task: Search proxy endpoint for an internal chat tool

method: Codex CLI added a FastAPI router with a POST handler that calls TavilyClient.search with include_answer true, then pytest with a mocked client, and a single manual curl at the end. Run from a Linux dev box.
limitations: Live call checked once by hand; the proxy has no rate limiting in front of it during this run.

summary: Claude Code ran fifty searches from a Jupyter notebook to compare two query phrasings across 25 questions; the question-style phrasing returned more reference-site hits. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The question-style phrasing returned more hits from reference sites, while the keyword phrasing returned more news items.
Running the cells in order produced the same tables on rerun, which made the comparison easy to repeat.

context.task: Compare two query phrasings on 25 questions

method: Claude Code ran fifty searches from a Jupyter notebook using the Python client, grouped the returned domains by phrasing, and printed counts per domain type. The notebook stayed on the author's laptop.
limitations: Twenty-five questions from one domain; domain types were labeled by the agent, not checked by a second reader.

summary: aider built a daily newsletter digest from Tavily results with max_results 8 and topic news, and the first generated file had eight linked items with dates. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Eight items came back with links and dates, and two needed their titles shortened to fit the email template.

context.task: Daily newsletter digest from news search

method: aider wrote a Python script that calls TavilyClient.search with topic news and max_results 8, then renders the results into an HTML email body. Run once from a Linux shell.
limitations: Single digest run; the email was not sent and was only previewed locally.

summary: A custom research agent takes Tavily results and passes them to a local reranker; across three runs the time to first answer was about 14 seconds. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The search step took a small share of the total time, and the reranker and model call took most of the rest.
Reranking moved one primary source above a news roundup on two of the three questions.

context.task: Research answers with reranked sources

method: Custom agent in Python calls TavilyClient.search with max_results 10, passes content snippets to a local cross-encoder reranker, and keeps the top three for the answer prompt. Ran three questions on one machine.
limitations: Three questions on one machine; the reranker was not compared against a no-rerank baseline.

summary: Cursor's first run of the Tavily script returned 401 because TAVILY_API_KEY was not exported in the shell; after exporting it in the same terminal, the search returned hits. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The first call failed with 401 and gave no hint that the variable was empty, so the agent had to print the environment to find it.
Exporting the variable in the same shell session fixed the call on the second attempt.

context.task: Script that searches a topic list

method: Cursor wrote a Python script with TavilyClient and ran it from an integrated terminal. The first run came from a shell where the variable was unset; the second run followed an export in that terminal.
limitations: One macOS terminal; the same variable set in a shell profile was not checked for new terminals.

summary: Devin's first search call failed with 401 because the key pasted into the secret store had a trailing space; trimming it and rerunning the job returned results. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The key looked correct in the UI, and the trailing space only showed up after the agent printed the key length.
The rerun passed after trimming, and the log showed the first hit list for the same query.

context.task: Competitor news job with first results

method: Devin wrote a Python script that reads TAVILY_API_KEY from the sandbox secret store, calls search for two competitor queries, and logs the response. Ran once, fixed the variable, and ran again.
limitations: Key checked in one sandbox; other secret stores and their whitespace handling were not compared.

summary: aider fired 60 searches in parallel from a bash loop, hit 429 responses on the first burst, and recovered after a sequential run with a short pause between requests. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Roughly a third of the parallel calls came back 429, and the response bodies were not parsed, so the failures went unnoticed at first.
A sequential loop with a one-second pause finished all 60 queries with no 429 responses.

context.task: Parallel topic sweep for a weekly index

method: aider wrote a bash loop that backgrounds one curl per topic, then reran the topics in a sequential loop with a one-second pause. Run from a Linux shell.
limitations: One sweep of sixty topics on a single shared key; no test of the concurrency level that triggers the limit.

summary: Goose passed include_domains as one comma-separated string, got an error response, and switched to a list before the second run returned hits. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The string value produced an error response on the first call, and the error text pointed at the request body rather than the key.
The parameter description asks for a list, which the agent only checked after the error.

context.task: Restrict a news search to two outlets

method: Goose called TavilyClient.search with include_domains as one string of two outlets, read the error, then changed the argument to a Python list and reran the same query. Run from a macOS terminal.
limitations: Two outlets in one filter; longer lists were not tested after the change.

summary: Cline's Next.js edge route failed at build because a dependency pulled in Node-only modules; moving the route to the Node runtime fixed the deploy on the second try. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The build failed on a Node-only module import inside the edge route, and the error named the import path rather than the runtime.
Setting the route to the Node runtime removed the build error, and the endpoint answered with results on the first call.

context.task: Search endpoint for a Next.js app

method: Cline added a route handler that calls the JS client, deployed a preview build, read the build error, and switched the route to the Node runtime before a second preview build.
limitations: One preview deploy; production builds on a different Next.js setting were not checked.

summary: Windsurf imported the client under a guessed class name, got an ImportError, and the second attempt with the documented class name ran the topic search without errors. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The guessed class name raised ImportError at module load, so the failure happened before any request was sent.
The quickstart import line matched the class the agent eventually used, and the first search returned five results.

context.task: Topic search helper for a notes tool

method: Windsurf wrote a helper that imports a guessed class from the tavily package, ran it, corrected the import to TavilyClient, and reran the same query with max_results 5. Run in a Windows terminal.
limitations: One helper in one terminal; the import fix was not checked on other Python installs.

summary: Claude Code's advanced search calls timed out at 30 seconds in a sandbox, and basic depth finished every query, so the pipeline dropped to basic and completed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Four advanced calls hit the agent's 30-second client timeout, and the same queries returned in about a second at basic depth.
Falling back to basic depth for the rest of the run kept all queries finishing, though the content per result was shorter.

context.task: Batch research queries in a sandbox

method: Claude Code ran a batch of twenty queries with search_depth advanced on the Python client inside a sandbox with a 30-second timeout, then reran the timed-out queries with search_depth basic. Free plan key.
limitations: One sandbox with a 30-second client timeout; a longer timeout might have let advanced depth finish.

summary: OpenHands' results writer crashed on a Windows console with a UnicodeEncodeError for a non-Latin headline; forcing UTF-8 output on the file write let the run finish. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Printing a headline with non-Latin characters raised UnicodeEncodeError in the default console encoding, after the search had already returned.
Writing the results file with explicit UTF-8 encoding and printing a safe copy to the console fixed the run.

context.task: Save news search results to a local digest

method: OpenHands ran a news topic search with the Python client and wrote the results to a text file, then printed them to a Windows console. The print step failed on a non-Latin title, and the file was rewritten with UTF-8.
limitations: One Windows console and one topic; other locales and terminals were not checked.

summary: A custom TypeScript agent sent the key as a query parameter instead of the bearer header and got 401 on each call; moving it into the header restored results. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The query parameter form returned 401 on every call, while the same body with the header returned results.
The auth section shows the header form first, which the agent had skipped while copying an older snippet.

context.task: Tool wrapper for a support agent

method: Custom agent builds a fetch call to the search endpoint with the key in the query string, copied from an older snippet, then moves it into an Authorization header with the Bearer scheme. Run from a local Node process.
limitations: Single agent process on a laptop; the older snippet was not checked against the current docs.

summary: Devin's weekly search job failed DNS resolution on every call from the sandbox, so no query reached the search service, and the run ended with a note in the repo. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Each call failed name resolution before any connection opened, so the client never reached the request step.
The note in the repo listed the failing command and the error class, which was enough for a reviewer to reproduce it.

context.task: Weekly search job for a sales newsletter

method: Devin ran the Python job with TavilyClient inside its sandbox, retried each query with backoff, and wrote a repo note when all retries failed. No other network was tried in this run.
limitations: Only the sandbox network was tried, so whether the search service itself was reachable from elsewhere is unknown.

summary: aider's extract step returned short or empty bodies for most of the 12 pages in its list, and the run stopped before a summary was written for the digest. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Nine of twelve pages returned under two hundred characters, mostly cookie notices or app-shell text.
The agent tried two URL variants and then stopped instead of switching to search snippets for the digest.

context.task: Digest summaries from twelve article pages

method: aider wrote a Node script that posts twelve page urls to the extract endpoint through the JS client and prints the character count per page. Run from a Linux shell.
limitations: Twelve pages from news and blog sites; no check of which pages render their text on the client.

summary: OpenHands ran advanced-depth searches in a retry loop on a Free plan key until the usage limit blocked further calls; the run stopped with 60 of 200 queries done. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: After about sixty advanced-depth calls, the remaining queries were rejected for usage, and the retry loop kept spending its budget on them.
The retry loop treated the usage rejection like a timeout, so it never switched to basic depth for the remaining queries.

context.task: Competitor sweep of 200 queries

method: OpenHands wrote a Python loop with search_depth advanced for all 200 queries, a retry wrapper with backoff on any error, and no fallback depth. Ran on a Linux server with a Free plan key.
limitations: One batch on a Free plan key; no paid plan run was made to compare how quotas reset.

summary: Goose's search batch was cut off repeatedly by a VPN that dropped idle connections, and the run was stopped by hand after repeated reconnects without finishing the query list. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Long-running calls failed with connection reset errors whenever the VPN dropped the socket, which happened roughly every few minutes.
The agent restarted the batch from the top each time instead of resuming from the last saved query.

context.task: Batch search over 80 queries on a laptop

method: Goose ran a Python batch of eighty queries with the Tavily client on a laptop connected to a corporate VPN. Each reset restarted the loop from query one, and the run was stopped by hand.
limitations: One VPN and one laptop; the same batch from an unmanaged network was not run for comparison.

summary: Cursor's search route fanned out six queries in parallel on a serverless function, the platform cut the call at its time limit, and the agent gave up before reducing the fan-out. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The deployed route returned a gateway timeout on the three most recent attempts, while the local server answered in about four seconds.
The agent kept changing retry settings and never tried a single query per request, which likely would have fit the limit.

context.task: Multi-query search button on a marketing site

method: Cursor wired six parallel Tavily calls inside one Next.js route handler and deployed it to a Vercel preview. It retried with different settings on each deploy until the run was stopped by hand.
limitations: Preview deploy only, on one plan tier; the time limit on other plans was not measured.

summary: Codex CLI assumed every result carried a raw_content string, hit a null on one page, and stopped after two fix attempts that did not address the crash. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The crash came from a None value in the raw field on one result, which the code read as a string.
The first two patches only wrapped the print step, so the failing dictionary access stayed in place and the run ended.

context.task: Parse search results into a notes database

method: Codex CLI wrote a parser over Tavily results with include_raw_content enabled, then patched the print wrapper twice after a TypeError. The loop never changed the field access that broke.
limitations: One parser against a single query's result set; the other queries were not run after the failure.

summary: Claude Code's Tavily script never started on a Windows laptop because the python on PATH was the Store alias, and the run ended before the client was installed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The python command opened the Store page instead of running, so pip never installed the client and no script ran.
Most of the run went to finding which interpreter the shell used, and the agent did not switch to the py launcher.

context.task: Install and run topic search on a Windows laptop

method: Claude Code tried to run pip and python from a PowerShell session on a Windows 11 laptop, read the version output, and stopped after two failed invocations. No virtual environment was created.
limitations: One Windows laptop with a default Store install; a manual Python install was not tried in this run.

summary: Subscription renewal workflow sleeps until the next billing date, charges through an activity, and loops. The test ran three renewal cycles on a local dev server, each compressed to about two minutes. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The loop computed each sleep duration from workflow.now(), and the dev server timeline showed every timer firing at the expected offset.
The charge activity set startToCloseTimeout and a retry policy with a small attempt cap, which matched the stub used in the test.

context.task: Renew subscriptions on a billing cycle

method: Claude Code in a TypeScript project using @temporalio/workflow, @temporalio/activity and @temporalio/worker. Wrote a renewal workflow, an activity that calls a stub charge function, and a worker entry file. Started the dev server with the temporal CLI and ran three cycles.
limitations: The charge activity was a stub and no real payment calls were made; the cycle used minutes instead of calendar months.

summary: Nightly ETL runs as a Temporal Schedule that starts a workflow with a date-based workflow id. A manual start with the same id was rejected while the day's run was still open. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: client.schedule.create with a cron spec registered the schedule, and the UI listed the next action time without a separate deploy step.
Deriving the workflow id from the run date kept each day to one execution, and the manual start failed with an already-started error.

context.task: Run nightly ETL from a staging extract

method: Cursor agent in a TypeScript repo connected to a Temporal Cloud namespace over TLS. Wrote an ETL workflow with three activities, created a schedule with a cron spec through the client, then started a manual run with the same workflow id to test the conflict.
limitations: Staging extract of about a dozen tables; no full-volume load or schedule pause and resume was tested.

summary: Python OCR pipeline runs three activities per scanned page and starts one child workflow per document. A folder of forty scanned PDFs finished, and the slowest activity took most of the wall time. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: One child workflow per document kept the parent history short, and the UI showed each document as its own run tree.
The OCR activity sent no heartbeats in the first version, so the agent added one heartbeat call per page to keep long scans visible.

context.task: OCR scanned documents page by page

method: Codex CLI in a Python project with the temporalio package. Defined a document workflow that starts one child workflow per document, with OCR and text-cleanup activities. Ran it against a dev server with a folder of forty scanned PDFs.
limitations: The OCR call was replaced by a local stub with a fixed delay; real OCR accuracy and throughput were not measured.

summary: Email verification workflow waits on a confirm signal with a deadline using condition. The test shortened the deadline to 30 seconds and ran one path where the signal arrived and one where the deadline passed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The confirm signal handler set a flag, and condition with a timeout returned true as soon as the flag flipped.
When the deadline passed, condition returned false and the workflow marked the link as expired and completed.

context.task: Verify email addresses with a timed confirm signal

method: Aider in a TypeScript repo. Wrote a verification workflow that waits on a defineSignal handler with condition and a timeout, a start route in Express, and two test runs from a script: one that sends the signal and one that waits.
limitations: Test deadline was 30 seconds rather than 24 hours; timer behavior across worker restarts was not tested.

summary: Go inventory reservation saga reserves stock per line and runs compensating releases when a later reservation fails. A fixture with one out-of-stock line drove the compensation path, and the four earlier lines were released in reverse. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The compensation loop ran over the reserved lines in reverse, and each release activity carried its own retry policy.
The out-of-stock result was returned as a non-retryable application error, so the reservation activity did not retry the same line.

context.task: Reserve inventory lines with compensation on failure

method: Claude Code in a Go module using the Temporal Go SDK. Wrote a reservation workflow that calls one activity per line, keeps a stack of reserved lines, and calls release activities in reverse when a reservation fails. Ran the test suite with a fixture that forced one out-of-stock line.
limitations: Single-warehouse fixture with five lines; no concurrent reservations against the same stock were run.

summary: Refund approval workflow pauses until a reviewer signal arrives, then runs the refund activity. A reject decision ends the workflow with a clear result, and both paths were tested locally. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The approve and reject signals were separate handlers that set a decision field, and the workflow read that field before continuing.
A query handler returned the pending decision state while the workflow waited, and a small polling script read it during the test.

context.task: Gate refunds behind a reviewer decision

method: Goose agent in a TypeScript project. Created a workflow with approve and reject signal handlers and a status query, a refund activity behind the approval gate, and a small CLI that sends signals to a running workflow id.
limitations: Refund activity was a logging stub; reviewer identity checks and audit storage were not part of the run.

summary: Webhook receiver in Python starts a workflow per event id and forwards later status webhooks as signals. A replayed start webhook returned the existing run id instead of creating a second run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The handler caught the already-started error and returned the existing run id, so the replayed webhook got a 200 response without a second run.
Status webhooks were forwarded as signals using the run id from the lookup table, and the workflow logged each one in arrival order.

context.task: Forward provider webhook events into a running workflow

method: Cline in a FastAPI service with the temporalio client. Wrote a route that starts a workflow using the event id as workflow id, a status route that sends a signal, and replayed two saved webhook bodies with curl.
limitations: Two saved webhook bodies only; signature verification and out-of-order delivery across many events were not exercised.

summary: Video transcode activity runs ffmpeg for each rendition and sends heartbeats with the current frame count. A 14-minute clip produced all three renditions without any timeout firing. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Heartbeat details carried the frame count, so the dashboard showed progress while the activity ran instead of one long spinner.
A heartbeat timeout of 60 seconds was set next to the start-to-close timeout, so a stalled ffmpeg process would be retried instead of hanging.

context.task: Transcode uploaded video into three renditions

method: Windsurf in a pnpm workspace on Ubuntu. Wrote a transcode activity that shells out to ffmpeg for three renditions, calls heartbeat with the frame count every few seconds, and ran a worker against a local dev server with a 14-minute sample clip.
limitations: Single sample clip on one machine; GPU encoding and multi-file concurrency were not part of this run.

summary: Ran the temporal CLI list and show commands against a dev server to confirm three test workflows completed and none were still running. The printed event order matched the activity order in the workflow code. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: temporal workflow show printed each event with its id and type, which made the activity order easy to compare against the workflow code.
The list command took a query string, and the agent used it to filter for running executions and confirm there were none.

context.task: Check workflow history from the command line

method: OpenHands agent on a Linux box with the temporal CLI installed. Started a local dev server, ran three test workflows from a script, then used workflow list and workflow show to confirm final statuses and read the activity order.
limitations: Checked only three local workflows on a dev server; no namespace with real history volume was inspected.

summary: Tenant fan-out workflow starts one child workflow per tenant and collects the results in the parent. The fixture with eight tenants completed, and each child returned its own summary object. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Each tenant child used a workflow id prefixed with the tenant id, so the UI grouped the runs by tenant without extra tags.
Collecting the child result promises with Promise.all gave the parent all eight summaries, and it wrote one row at the end.

context.task: Run a per-tenant report fan out

method: Claude Code in a TypeScript monorepo with workflows and activities in separate files. Wrote a parent workflow that calls startChild per tenant id, a child that loads the tenant rows and writes a summary, and ran the fixture of eight tenants on a dev server.
limitations: Eight synthetic tenants on a single dev server; cross-tenant load and large fan-out sizes were not tested.

summary: Trial reminder workflow sleeps for a set delay, then sends a reminder and answers a status query. The test used a 20-second trial, and the query returned the current step while the timer was running. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The query handler answered while the workflow was inside workflow.sleep, so the status endpoint returned the current step without waiting.
Reminders fired at the expected offsets in the dev server history, within a second or two of the planned wait.

context.task: Send a trial reminder after a fixed delay

method: Cursor agent in a Python project with the temporalio package and a FastAPI status route. Wrote a workflow with workflow.sleep, a reminder activity, and a status query. Ran the test on a local dev server with a 20-second trial length.
limitations: Used a 20-second trial length; sleep behavior across days and across worker restarts was not checked.

summary: Polling workflow checks a job status on a timer and calls continueAsNew every batch of checks to keep history short. The test ran four workflow runs and carried the job id into each new run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The loop passed the job id and cursor into continueAsNew, and each new run started with the same job id and a fresh history.
The code sleeps one minute between checks, and the test shortened that to ten seconds so the four runs finished quickly.

context.task: Poll a long-running external job until it finishes

method: Custom SDK agent in a TypeScript service calling the Temporal client. Wrote a polling workflow that checks status through an activity, sleeps, and calls continueAsNew every 25 checks. Ran it against a mock job endpoint that finished on the fourth run.
limitations: Mock job endpoint returned fixed states; real job durations and rate limits from the external API were not exercised.

summary: Go service registers a Temporal Schedule that runs a report workflow every weekday morning. The schedule was paused and resumed once from the CLI, and the next run followed the resume. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The calendar spec with weekdays and an 08:00 hour produced the first fire at the next weekday morning shown in the schedule description.
Pausing the schedule from the CLI stopped new runs, and resuming it created the next run at the next matching time.

context.task: Run a weekday morning report on a schedule

method: Codex CLI in a Go service using the Temporal Go client. Created a schedule with a calendar spec for weekdays at 08:00, wrote the report workflow, and used the temporal CLI to pause and resume the schedule against a dev server.
limitations: Dev server clock only; daylight saving changes and multi-timezone schedules were not tested.

summary: Workflow update changes the maximum attempts for a running import without restarting it. The update returned the stored value to the caller, and a zero value was rejected by the validator. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The update handler stored the new maxAttempts value and returned it to the caller once the handler finished.
A validator rejected a zero value before the update was recorded, and the caller received the rejection message.

context.task: Change retry settings on a running import

method: Devin in a TypeScript project. Added defineUpdate with a validator and a handler that stores the new retry count, then called the update from a client script against a running import on the dev server.
limitations: Single running import on a dev server; the update was not tested against a workflow started before the handler existed.

summary: Python activity marks an invalid-address error as non-retryable in its retry policy, so the workflow stopped after one attempt instead of retrying. The fixture address was chosen to hit that error. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Listing the error type in non_retryable_error_types stopped the retry loop after one attempt, and the workflow failed with the activity error attached.
The name in the list had to match the exception class name exactly, which the agent confirmed by reading the error type field on the raised failure.

context.task: Stop retrying invalid addresses in a Python activity

method: Aider in a Python package with temporalio. Set a RetryPolicy with non_retryable_error_types for an InvalidAddress exception, wrote an activity that raises it for a bad fixture address, and ran the workflow on a dev server.
limitations: One fixture address on a dev server; transient network errors were not part of this test, so the default retry path was not exercised.

summary: Local Temporal dev server started with a database file so workflow history survived a restart. After the restart, the completed run was still listed with its full event history. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Starting the dev server with a database filename kept completed history after a restart; without it, the agent expected the in-memory default to reset.
The gRPC address on 7233 and the web UI on 8233 were both reachable, and the worker config pointed at the 7233 address.

context.task: Keep local dev history across restarts

method: Claude Code on macOS with the temporal CLI. Started the dev server with a db filename, ran a sample workflow to completion, stopped the server, restarted it with the same file, and listed the workflow from the CLI.
limitations: Single sample workflow on macOS; no multi-workflow load or CLI upgrade between restarts was tested.

summary: Workflow change added a new activity behind a patched check so running executions kept their old path. A replay of a saved history from before the change passed afterward. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Wrapping the new activity call in patched with a version id kept the old event history replaying without a nondeterminism error.
Feeding an exported history file into the replay helper confirmed the old execution still matched the new code path.

context.task: Add an activity to a workflow with running executions

method: Windsurf in a pnpm TypeScript project. Added a patched guard around a new notification activity, exported a history from a completed run in the dev server, and ran the replay helper against that file before and after the change.
limitations: Only one workflow type was replayed; the version marker was left in place for a later cleanup pass.

summary: Worker connects to a Temporal Cloud namespace with an API key over TLS, with the namespace and key read from environment variables. The first connection succeeded and a test workflow ran on the cloud task queue. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The cloud address, TLS option and API key connected on the first try, and the worker began polling the task queue right after startup.
The key lived only in an environment variable on the worker host and was kept out of the repository and the workflow payload.

context.task: Connect a worker to Temporal Cloud

method: Cline in a TypeScript worker project. Changed the connection options to the cloud address with TLS and an API key, read the namespace and key from the environment, and started one test workflow from a client script.
limitations: Used one namespace on a trial account; key rotation and multi-region failover were not part of the test.

summary: Retention job checks for a cancel request between batches and exits cleanly when one arrives. The test cancelled a run during its second batch, and the run closed as canceled with a partial deleted count. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The batch loop ran inside a cancellation scope, so the in-flight activity finished and no further batch started after the cancel.
A finally block recorded the partial deleted count before the run closed, so the final state showed how far the cleanup got.

context.task: Stop a retention cleanup cleanly on cancel

method: Devin in a TypeScript project. Wrapped the batch loop in a cancellation scope, added a finally block that records the deleted count, then started a run on a dev server and called cancel during batch two.
limitations: Cancel tested on one dev run with a small batch size; a cancel during a long-running heartbeat was not exercised.

summary: Deadline check used Date.now inside the workflow and passed on the first run. After the worker restarted, replay threw a nondeterminism error, and switching to the workflow clock fixed it. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Replay after a worker restart threw a nondeterminism error at the deadline check, because Date.now returned a different value than the recorded history.
Switching to the workflow clock and rerunning the replay test passed, and a review pass flagged two more Date calls in the same file.

context.task: Enforce a deadline inside a long workflow

method: Devin in a TypeScript project. Wrote a deadline check using Date.now in the workflow, ran it on a dev server, restarted the worker mid-run, and replayed the history. Replaced Date.now with the workflow clock and reran the replay test.
limitations: Single deadline workflow; other sources of nondeterminism such as random ids were not audited in full.

summary: Python shipping workflow failed at its first activity call because no start-to-close timeout was set. The agent added the timeout to each call, and the second run completed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The execute_activity call raised a validation error about missing timeouts before any activity was scheduled, so the workflow never reached its first step.
The message named the missing timeout argument, which made the fix a one-line change in each activity call.

context.task: Run a three-step shipping workflow in Python

method: Codex CLI in a Python package with temporalio. Wrote a shipping workflow with three activities, ran it on a dev server, read the failed workflow task in the UI, and added start_to_close_timeout to each execute_activity call before rerunning.
limitations: Three stub activities on a dev server; retry policy tuning and schedule-to-close timeouts were left at their defaults.

summary: LLM summarization activity received HTTP 429 from the model API on two runs. Its retry policy with backoff carried the workflow through, and the summary landed on the third attempt. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Two 429 responses surfaced as activity failures; the retry policy waited with backoff and the third attempt returned a summary.
Marking only the input validation error as non-retryable kept the rate limit path retrying, which is what the agent wanted.

context.task: Summarize long documents with an LLM activity

The onUploadError callback received the error object, and reading its message property was enough for the toast.

context.task: Reject anonymous uploads with a readable message

method: Claude Code edited a Next.js App Router repo. Added a session check to the middleware of the file router that throws UploadThingError with a short message, wired onUploadError to a toast, and tested signed-in and signed-out uploads.
limitations: Tested with two local accounts; rate limits and expired sessions were not exercised.

summary: Goose built a bulk uploader for up to ten PDFs at once with per-file progress. All ten files finished in one batch, and each row drew its own progress bar. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A maxFileCount of 10 on the pdf route stopped an eleventh selection in the dropzone before any upload started.
Per-file progress came from the client hook, which was enough to draw one bar per row without polling anything.

context.task: Upload up to ten PDFs in one batch

method: Goose in a React app with a pdf route limited to ten files. Rendered a list of progress rows from the upload hook, uploaded a batch of ten sample PDFs from a local folder, and checked the stored keys afterwards.
limitations: Ten small PDFs under 1 MB each; large batches and slow networks were not tested.

summary: A custom agent pushed 23 generated CSV exports from a worker with UTApi uploadFiles, in one backfill run. Every export came back with a key and none failed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Sequential uploadFiles calls kept the exports in date order, and the manifest matched the folder listing.
Each uploadFiles result came back as a data or error object, and the worker wrote the key for every success into a manifest file.

context.task: Backfill 23 daily CSV exports

method: A custom SDK agent running a Node worker. Looped over 23 export files on disk, called utapi.uploadFiles once per file with a File built from the bytes, and wrote each returned key to a manifest JSON.
limitations: Exports were 1 to 3 MB each; larger files and parallel uploads were not measured.

summary: OpenHands rendered an image grid from rows that onUploadComplete saved to Postgres. The grid showed the new files on the first reload after the callback finished. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The row insert ran inside onUploadComplete, so the grid only showed a file once the server callback had finished.
The browser kept an old thumbnail for one reload after a replacement, and a query string on the image URL cleared it.

context.task: Show uploaded images in a gallery grid

method: OpenHands in a Next.js App Router app with Postgres through Drizzle. onUploadComplete inserted a row with the file key and user id, and a server component queried the table for the grid. Reloaded the page after three uploads.
limitations: Three test images on one account; the grid was not checked with long lists or pagination.

summary: Aider placed an UploadButton inside a Server Component and the build failed on the hook call. The later attempts moved the import around, and the run stopped before the component became a client component. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The upload component uses hooks, so the file that renders it needs a client boundary, and the agent never added one before the build failed.
The build error named the hook but not the page file that rendered the component, so the agent searched the repo for the hook name.

context.task: Add an upload button to a server-rendered settings page

limitations: One page and one component; a client wrapper at the layout level was not tried.

summary: Windsurf sent a PDF to a route that only allowed images, and the upload was refused. The agent did not add a PDF route before the run ended. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The router accepted only the image key, so a PDF selected in the dropzone was refused with a file type message.
The agent loosened the accept attribute in the HTML input and retried, which did not change the server-side check.

context.task: Accept PDF attachments on an upload form

method: Windsurf in a React form that calls generateReactHelpers against a router with only an image route. Selected a PDF in the input, watched the upload fail, changed the accept attribute twice, then stopped.
limitations: One form and one browser; the PDF route was never written, so the same flow with a pdf route is untested.

summary: Cline added a video route with a 64MB cap and a single file limit, then uploaded a 41 MB clip from the test folder. The stored size matched the local file exactly. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The video key accepted an mp4 file at 41 MB without any extra configuration in the router.
The stored size matched the local file byte for byte, which the agent confirmed by comparing the metadata with the file on disk.

context.task: Accept short product demo videos

method: Cline in a Next.js repo. Added a video route with maxFileSize 64MB and maxFileCount 1 to the file router, rendered an UploadButton on a test page, and uploaded a 41 MB mp4 from the test folder.
limitations: One 41 MB clip on one machine; transcoding and playback in other browsers were not checked.

summary: Goose wrote an onUploadComplete handler that returned nothing, so the browser got empty serverData and the page could not find the new file key. Returning the key fixed it on the second try. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Whatever onUploadComplete returns is passed to the client as serverData, and an undefined return left the page with nothing to read.
The agent had written the callback as a logging-only function, which is why no return value existed in the first version.

context.task: Show the new file key on the page after upload

method: Goose in a Next.js App Router app with a file router that logs in onUploadComplete. The page read serverData from the upload result, found it undefined, then added a return with the file key and reran the upload.
limitations: Only one file per upload was tested, so per-file server data for batches was not checked.

summary: Codex added an admin page that renames display names in the database and leaves the UploadThing keys untouched. Renames saved on the first submit and the stored key stayed the same. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Keeping the display name in its own column meant renames never touched the storage key, so existing links kept working.
The server action validated the new name length before the update, which kept empty names out of the table.

context.task: Let admins rename uploaded files

method: Codex CLI in a Next.js App Router app with Drizzle. Added a display_name column, wrote a server action that updates only that column, and tested renames on three rows from the admin page.
limitations: Three rows in a development database; concurrent edits to the same file were not tested.

summary: A custom agent skipped the React helpers and posted multipart form data to the upload route by hand. The route kept answering with 400 errors, and the run ended with no upload completed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The route expects the request shape the React helpers send, so a plain multipart POST was rejected before the file reached the router.
The agent changed the field names three times and never read the upload client source to check the expected shape.

context.task: Upload a file from a script to the upload route

method: A custom SDK agent with a Python requests script posting multipart form data to the upload route of a local Next.js server. Changed the field names several times and reran after each change until the time budget ran out.
limitations: One local server; the upload route was not inspected from the server side, so the exact rejection reason is unconfirmed.

summary: OpenHands resized uploaded photos to 1600 pixels wide with sharp inside a route handler, then sent the resized buffer to uploadFiles. Output files came out noticeably smaller than the originals. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Resizing happened before the upload call, so the stored object was already the smaller file and no client code changed.
Metadata stripping came from the sharp pipeline by default, so location tags from the phone photos did not reach storage.

context.task: Shrink phone photos before storing them

method: OpenHands in a Next.js route handler. Read the upload with arrayBuffer, ran sharp resize to width 1600 with JPEG output, wrapped the buffer in a File, and called uploadFiles. Checked two sample photos before and after.
limitations: Two JPEG phone photos; PNG and HEIC inputs and very large images were not tested.

summary: Windsurf's upload hit a size rejection on a 6 MB photo, because the React hint said 8 MB but the route capped files at 4MB. Raising the route cap to 8MB fixed it on the second attempt. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The help text and the route cap are separate values, so they can disagree without any build error.
The client showed a generic upload failure, and the size reason appeared only in the server log.

context.task: Accept 6 MB profile photos

method: Windsurf in a React app with an image route capped at 4MB. The help text under the dropzone said 8 MB. Picked a 6 MB photo, read the server log for the rejection, then changed the route cap to 8MB and reran the upload.
limitations: One photo size and one browser; larger files near the cap and other image formats were not tested.

summary: Claude Code mocked the upload hook in Vitest so component tests could render the button without network calls. The suite passed on the first run with the mock in place. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Mocking the hook module at the import path kept the component code unchanged, and the test file needed about 30 lines.
Route modules read environment variables at import time, so the test setup sets a placeholder value before the router file loads.

context.task: Test the upload button without hitting the network

method: Claude Code in a React repo with Vitest and Testing Library. Wrote vi.mock for the module that exports the upload hook, set a placeholder environment value in the setup file, and rendered the button in one test.
limitations: One component and one test file; end-to-end upload behavior in a real browser was not covered.

summary: Devin pushed a batch of large test files until the account showed a plan quota notice on the fourth upload. The run stopped there, and the later uploads never completed. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The account on the free plan hit a storage quota notice partway through the batch, and new uploads failed until the quota was freed.
The notice appeared in the dashboard and in the client response, but the agent only noticed it after it had retried each file three times.

context.task: Upload a batch of large test files

method: Devin in a cloud sandbox with a Node script that called the upload route for 12 files of about 25 MB each. Retried failed files three times each and stopped when the session timer ran out.
limitations: One free plan account in one session; paid plan behavior and quota reset timing were not checked.

summary: Aider added a join table that links uploaded file keys to users and projects. Inserts worked on the first run, and a project delete cascaded to its file links only. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Keeping the file key as a plain text column meant the join rows never depended on UploadThing for lookups.
The cascade on project delete removed the link rows and left the stored files in place, which matched the plan to clean files later.

context.task: Link uploaded files to users and projects

method: Aider in a Next.js app with Drizzle migrations. Added a file_links table with user_id, project_id and file_key columns, generated the migration, applied it to a local Postgres, and inserted two test links.
limitations: Two test links in a local database; the cleanup job for orphaned stored files was not written.

summary: Cline's Docker image started cleanly, but every upload returned 500 until the token was passed as a runtime environment variable instead of a build argument. The next container run succeeded. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The 500 showed in the container logs with the route name only, and the missing variable was not named in the message.

limitations: One VM and one image tag; orchestration platforms and secret managers were not evaluated.

summary: Goose moved the file router into a shared package that two Next.js apps import. Both apps uploaded through the same route name, and the types came through without extra config. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

Each app still needed its own route file that calls createRouteHandler with the shared router, which the agent kept as a thin wrapper.

The agent retried over a dozen times with changed timeouts, which did nothing, instead of reading the router config it had just edited.

summary: Cursor added an upload status panel that reads the isUploading flag from the hook and disables submit until the upload finishes. The panel behaved correctly on a slow throttled connection. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

context.task: Disable submit until the upload is saved

Exporting only the router type from a separate file let the client read the route names without importing any server code.

summary: Aider's onUploadComplete wrote to a local SQLite file, and parallel uploads caused SQLITE_BUSY errors. Switching the callback to a queue with a single writer fixed it on the second attempt. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

Routing the inserts through one async queue removed the busy errors, and the batch finished without retries from the client.

context.task: Record uploads in SQLite while uploading in parallel

method: Aider in a Node service using better-sqlite3. Ran a batch of eight parallel uploads, saw SQLITE_BUSY in the logs, then wrapped inserts in a small in-process queue and reran the same batch.
limitations: One batch of eight files on one machine; the queue was not tested across multiple server processes.

summary: Cline queued a thumbnail job after each upload finished, so the callback returned fast and the image work ran in a separate worker. Ten thumbnails were ready within a minute of the uploads. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The onUploadComplete handler only enqueued the job and returned, so the client was not held open while the image work ran.
All ten thumbnails finished within about a minute on the worker, and the job log recorded one row per file.

context.task: Generate thumbnails without slowing uploads

method: Cline in a Node service with a simple job table and a polling worker. Inserted a job row in onUploadComplete, the worker read it and wrote the thumbnail back under the same file key, and the test batch of ten images ran end to end.
limitations: Ten small test images; no failure path or retry for failed thumbnail jobs was exercised.

summary: Windsurf added an UploadButton story to Storybook with a mocked endpoint, so designers could click through the states without a live router. The story rendered idle, uploading and error states. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The story needed a stub for the upload hook, which the agent wrote after reading the component source.

summary: Goose's CI run failed because the upload route read the token at module load, and the test job had no token set yet. Moving the read into the handler body fixed the job on the second run. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The repository secret existed for deploy jobs only, so the test job needed its own secret mapping in the workflow file.

limitations: One workflow file and one test job; the deploy job and preview environments were not changed.

summary: Moved the welcome email out of the signup request by publishing a job to a Next.js route with three retries. The worker verified the signature and returned 200 on the first delivery. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The verification guide showed Receiver with both signing keys but did not say the body must be read as raw text before verify is called.

context.task: Offload welcome email sending

summary: Deliveries to the preview deployment returned 401 for every attempt, so the test was moved to the production alias. The next publish returned 200 on the first attempt. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

The delivery log listed each attempt with its status code, which made the 401 pattern clear after the second retry.

summary: Created a recurring schedule that calls a Remix action every five minutes to refresh a search index. The first run showed up in the logs within the five minute window. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: The first run landed 3 minutes and 40 seconds after the schedule was created, which fits a five minute cron with creation partway through the window.
The schedule view showed UTC only, so the agent confirmed the expression was evaluated in UTC before relying on it for business hours.

context.task: Refresh search index on a schedule

method: Cursor wrote a one-off script that calls client.schedules.create with a */5 * * * * cron and the action URL as destination, then listed schedules to confirm the entry and read the action log until the first run appeared.
limitations: One schedule watched for about ten minutes; no check across a deploy or a restart of the action host.

summary: Publishing to a localhost endpoint from the dev machine never reached the handler, and retries ran out with no delivery. The agent stopped without setting up a tunnel. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Every attempt to the localhost URL failed on the QStash side, and the delivery log showed the final state as failed after the configured retries.
The quickstart used localhost as a destination example without a note that QStash cannot call a private address.

context.task: Test job delivery locally

method: Cline wrote a publishJSON call pointing at a localhost route on port 3000, ran the Next.js dev server, published one message, and waited for the delivery log to show the final state.
limitations: No tunnel or preview deployment was tried, so only the localhost destination itself was tested.

summary: Added a FastAPI endpoint that verifies the Upstash-Signature header with the Python SDK before running an email digest job. Valid deliveries returned 200 and a tampered body returned 401. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: A delivery with a tampered body returned 401 from the verifier, while the untouched delivery returned 200 and ran the digest job once.
The endpoint read the request bytes before parsing JSON, which kept the signed body identical to what QStash sent.

context.task: Verify QStash deliveries in FastAPI

method: Codex CLI built a Receiver from the two signing keys in environment config, verified each request body against the Upstash-Signature header value, and ran pytest with one valid and one tampered request.
limitations: Local uvicorn server with pytest client calls; no real QStash delivery from the public internet was observed.

summary: Published one message to a URL group so three downstream endpoints received the same event. Each endpoint returned 200 and logged the same event ID. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: All three endpoints logged event id evt-2231 within the same minute, and none of them waited on another endpoint's slow response.
Creating the URL group needed a separate API call before publish, which the quickstart did not show in the same snippet.

context.task: Fan out order events to three services

summary: Signature verification failed with 401 because the route parsed the JSON body before calling the verifier. Reading the body as text first made the same deliveries pass. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Calling req.json() before Receiver.verify changed the bytes that were checked, so every valid delivery returned 401 at first.
Reading req.text() first and parsing afterwards let the verifier pass all five test deliveries on the rerun.

context.task: Verify deliveries in Next.js route

method: Cursor wrote the job route with req.json() at the top, sent five deliveries through a tunnel, read the 401 responses, switched to req.text(), verified the string, then parsed it with JSON.parse and reran the same five deliveries.
limitations: Five deliveries through a tunnel to one route; the failing path was not compared with other routes.

summary: Scheduled a 30 second delayed publish to send a reminder to a Cloudflare Worker endpoint. The Worker received each reminder after the delay and returned 200. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]

observations.observation: Deliveries arrived between 31 and 34 seconds after publish across five test runs, so the delay was honored with a small margin.
The Worker returned 200 before writing the reminder to storage, so a storage failure after the response would not trigger a QStash retry.

context.task: Send delayed reminder

method: Cline wrote a Hono Worker handler and a publish call with a 30 second delay, ran wrangler dev behind a tunnel, then published five messages and logged the arrival time of each delivery.
limitations: Five deliveries from one account through a tunnel; the delay was measured from the publish response, not from the queue's internal clock.

summary: All deliveries to the preview deployment returned 401 from the access gate, and the agent could not find a way to pass the gate from the test. The run ended with no successful deliveries. [SAMPLE FOR DEMO]
